questions.stem: A teacher wants to know how many hours students really spend on homework each night. She asks each student to say the number out loud in front of the whole class. What is the most likely problem with the data?
choices: Students may give answers that make them look good, so the reported hours may not be true
The question is not statistical, because the hours vary from one student to the next
The sample is too large to be useful, because every student in the class answered
Hours of homework are categorical data, so they cannot be compared
questions.answer: Students may give answers that make them look good, so the reported hours may not be true
questions.solution: Answering out loud in front of classmates and the teacher can push students to say what sounds best, which biases the data. Varying answers are what make a question statistical, a larger sample is not a problem, and hours are numerical data.

solve.answer: Students may give answers that make them look good, so the reported hours may not be true
solve.work: Public reporting causes response bias: students may inflate or shade answers.

questions.skill: Judging the credibility of a source
questions.stem: Which source is the most credible for finding the average number of students per class in a state's public schools?
choices: A social media post by an anonymous account that gives no sources
An advertisement from a company that sells school supplies
A classmate's estimate based on only her own class
A report from the state education agency that explains how its data were collected
questions.answer: A report from the state education agency that explains how its data were collected
questions.solution: A credible source is open about how its data were collected and covers the whole group. The other sources give no method, may have a reason to exaggerate, or look at only one class.

solve.answer: A report from the state education agency that explains how its data were collected
solve.work: An official agency report that documents its methods is the most credible; the others are anonymous, anecdotal or commercially motivated.

questions.skill: Choosing relevant variables
questions.stem: A student wants to predict the selling price of a house. Which variable is the LEAST useful for this?
choices: the size of the house in square feet
the favorite color of the owner
the number of bedrooms
the neighborhood
questions.answer: the favorite color of the owner
questions.solution: Size, number of bedrooms and neighborhood all affect what buyers pay. The owner's favorite color has no connection to the price.

solve.answer: the favorite color of the owner
solve.work: Size, bedrooms and neighborhood all relate to price; the owner's favorite color does not.

questions.skill: Judging the credibility of a data source
questions.stem: Tanya wants to know how much rain fell in Raleigh last month. Which source is the most trustworthy?
choices: Rain gauge records posted by a weather service
A neighbor who remembers it as a rainy month
A store poster that advertises rain jackets
A popular video titled "Wildest Weather Ever!"
questions.answer: Rain gauge records posted by a weather service
questions.solution: Measured records from a weather service are collected with instruments and a stated method. A memory, an ad and a catchy video title are not measurements.

solve.answer: Rain gauge records posted by a weather service
solve.work: Measured rain gauge records from a weather service are direct, documented data; the others are entertainment, advertising or memory.

questions.skill: Judging the credibility of a data source
questions.stem: A survey about the best sneaker brand was paid for by a sneaker company. Why should you be careful with its results?
choices: Companies are never able to collect any data about sneakers or shoes
The company could gain if the results favor its own sneakers
Sneakers are too hard to compare, so no survey could work
Surveys are only trustworthy when they are very short
questions.answer: The company could gain if the results favor its own sneakers
questions.solution: A source that profits from a certain result may be biased, so we look at how the data were collected. Companies can collect data, and length is not what makes a survey trustworthy.

solve.answer: The company could gain if the results favor its own sneakers
solve.work: Sponsor bias: the company benefits if results favor its brand.

questions.skill: Judging the credibility of a data source
questions.stem: Which detail makes a data source MORE trustworthy?
choices: It uses large, colorful pictures and bold headings
It was shared by many people on several different social media sites
It explains who collected the data and how it was collected
It uses many technical words and long, complicated sentences
questions.answer: It explains who collected the data and how it was collected
questions.solution: A trustworthy source tells you who collected the data and how, so that others can check it. Looks, popularity and technical words do not show that data are sound.

solve.answer: It explains who collected the data and how it was collected
solve.work: Transparency about who collected data and how raises trust; popularity, visuals and jargon do not.

questions.skill: Judging the credibility of a data source
questions.stem: Mia scores a website with a checklist: 1 point if it names its author, 1 point if it gives a date, 1 point if it lists where its data came from, and 1 point if it is NOT trying to sell a product. Website Q names its author, has no date, lists its data source, and sells a product. How many points does Website Q score?
questions.solution: Website Q earns 1 point for naming its author and 1 point for listing its data source. It has no date (0) and it sells a product (0). Total: 1 + 1 = 2 points.

solve.work: Author: 1. Date: 0. Data source: 1. Not selling: 0 (it sells). Total 2.

questions.skill: Judging the credibility of a data source
questions.stem: A school wants to know what its students think about a new lunch menu. Which survey result is the most likely to be reliable?
choices: Asking the 6 students sitting at one lunch table in the cafeteria today
Asking only the students who belong to the school's chess club team
Counting the answers of students who visit the school's website
Asking 150 students chosen at random from the school's list
questions.answer: Asking 150 students chosen at random from the school's list
questions.solution: A large group chosen at random from the whole school represents the students. A single table, one club, or people who choose to answer online may not be typical.

solve.answer: Asking 150 students chosen at random from the school's list
solve.work: A random sample of 150 from the full list is representative; the others are self-selected or tiny/biased groups.

questions.skill: Choosing relevant variables
questions.stem: A coach asks, "Does more practice time lead to more free throws made?" Which variable is the outcome being predicted?
choices: The number of free throws made
The minutes of practice time
The names of the players
The color of the basketball
questions.answer: The number of free throws made
questions.solution: Practice time is used to predict the number of free throws made, so free throws made is the outcome.

solve.answer: The number of free throws made
solve.work: Outcome (response) is free throws made; practice time is the predictor.

questions.skill: Choosing relevant variables
questions.stem: A baker wants to predict how many cups of hot chocolate she will sell each day. Which variable would help the most?
choices: The color of her apron
The outdoor temperature that day
The number of windows in her shop
The weight of her bag of flour
questions.answer: The outdoor temperature that day
questions.solution: Colder days probably mean more hot chocolate. The other variables have no clear link to sales of the drink.

solve.answer: The outdoor temperature that day
solve.work: Hot chocolate demand depends on temperature; others irrelevant.

questions.skill: Choosing relevant variables
questions.stem: Pat wants to see whether the age of a car affects its resale price. Which two columns of data does Pat need?
choices: Car color and resale price
Age of the car and number of doors
Age of the car and resale price
Number of doors and color of the car
questions.answer: Age of the car and resale price
questions.solution: To study the effect of age on price, Pat needs the age column and the price column.

solve.answer: Age of the car and resale price
solve.work: Need the explanatory variable (age) and response (resale price).

questions.skill: Choosing relevant variables
questions.stem: Dev wants to know whether the distance a student lives from school affects the time the trip takes. Which variable is NOT needed?
choices: The distance from the student's home to the school
The number of minutes that the trip takes
How the student travels (bus, bike or walking)
The student's favorite school subject
questions.answer: The student's favorite school subject
questions.solution: Distance and trip time are the two variables in the question, and the way of traveling may matter too. A favorite subject has nothing to do with trip time.

solve.answer: The student's favorite school subject
solve.issues: Soft: strictly, travel mode is also not needed for the two-variable question as asked, though it is clearly relevant. Intended answer is still clear.
solve.work: Distance and trip time are essential; travel mode is a relevant third variable; favorite subject is irrelevant.

questions.skill: Choosing relevant variables
questions.stem: Which question can be investigated using the variables "minutes of exercise per day" and "resting heart rate"?
choices: Do people who exercise more tend to have lower resting heart rates?
Which sport do people who exercise like to play the most?
Do people with calm hearts tend to have more brothers and sisters?
How much taller are people who exercise than people who do not?
questions.answer: Do people who exercise more tend to have lower resting heart rates?
questions.solution: Only the first question can be answered by comparing these two variables.

solve.answer: Do people who exercise more tend to have lower resting heart rates?
solve.work: Both variables appear only in the first question (exercise vs resting heart rate).

questions.skill: Evaluating a dataset for a question
questions.stem: Nia wants to know how long students at her own school take to get to school. Which data would answer her question best?
choices: Travel times from a random group of students at her school
Travel times of adults who drive to work in her town
The number of buses owned by her school and its district
The lengths of all the roads in the area near her school
questions.answer: Travel times from a random group of students at her school
questions.solution: Only travel times from students at her school match her question.

solve.answer: Travel times from a random group of students at her school
solve.work: Need travel times of students at her school; a random group of them answers it.

questions.skill: Evaluating a dataset for a question
questions.stem: In a dataset of plant heights, some values are in inches and others in centimeters, and the unit is not labeled. What should be done before comparing the heights?
choices: Compare them as they are, since all are heights
Find each value's unit and convert them all to one unit
Remove all of the rows that have the smaller numbers in them
Round every height to the nearest ten
questions.answer: Find each value's unit and convert them all to one unit
questions.solution: Values in different units cannot be compared directly, so first find the units and convert to a single one.

solve.answer: Find each value's unit and convert them all to one unit
solve.work: Mixed unlabeled units must be identified and converted to one unit before comparing.

questions.skill: Evaluating a dataset for a question
questions.stem: Which column of a student dataset is categorical?
choices: Number of siblings
Age in years
Favorite color
Minutes spent on homework
questions.answer: Favorite color
questions.solution: A categorical variable puts people in groups by a quality, such as a color. The other columns are measured or counted numbers.

solve.answer: Favorite color
solve.work: Favorite color is a category; the rest are numeric.

questions.skill: Evaluating a dataset for a question
questions.stem: Daily steps, in thousands, for seven days: 6, 7, 5, 6, 40, 7, 6. One value is most likely a typing error. What is that value?
questions.solution: Six of the values are between 5 and 7, while 40 is far away from them. A person is unlikely to take 40 thousand steps, so 40 is the likely error.

solve.work: Values cluster 5-7 thousand; 40 is the anomaly.

questions.skill: Splitting data by a third variable
questions.stem: Test scores and hours studied are recorded for ninth and tenth graders mixed together. Dani wants to see whether the pattern differs by grade. What should she do?
choices: Delete the tenth graders' scores
Plot each grade separately and compare
Add each student's hours and score together
Average the two grades into one number
questions.answer: Plot each grade separately and compare
questions.solution: Splitting the data by the third variable, grade, lets her compare the two patterns.

solve.answer: Plot each grade separately and compare
solve.work: To see if the pattern differs by grade, split by grade and plot each separately.

questions.skill: Splitting data by a third variable
questions.stem: Dani sorts the rows of a dataset into two piles: students who ride the bus to school and students who do not. Which variable did she split the data by?
choices: The student's test score
The student's grade level
How the student travels
The student's height
questions.answer: How the student travels
questions.solution: The two piles are made by how students get to school, so that is the splitting variable.

solve.answer: How the student travels
solve.work: Bus vs not bus is a split by mode of travel.

questions.skill: Using a third variable to improve a model
questions.stem: In the morning class, the line that predicts a test score is $y = 4x + 50$, where $x$ is the hours studied. What score does the line predict for a student who studied 5 hours?
questions.solution: Put $x = 5$ into the line: $y = 4(5) + 50 = 70$.

questions.skill: Using a third variable to improve a model
questions.stem: A single line fits all the data points badly. Which step uses a third variable to improve the model?
choices: Remove the third variable from the data
Draw a longer line through the same points
Fit a separate line for each group
Round all values
questions.answer: Fit a separate line for each group
questions.solution: Splitting the points by the third variable and fitting a line to each group can follow each group's pattern.

solve.answer: Fit a separate line for each group
solve.work: Using a grouping variable to fit separate lines per group improves the model.

questions.skill: Using a third variable to improve a model
questions.stem: Two groups each have their own line. Group 1: $y = 5x + 3$. Group 2: $y = 5x + 3$. What does this tell you about splitting the data by group?
choices: The two groups must both have been measured wrongly by someone
Splitting helps a lot, because there are now two separate lines
The slope of each of these two lines has to be exactly zero
Splitting does not help, since both groups share one line
questions.answer: Splitting does not help, since both groups share one line
questions.solution: Both groups have the same equation, so one line describes them equally well.

solve.answer: Splitting does not help, since both groups share one line
solve.work: Identical lines: the grouping variable makes no difference, so splitting does not help.

questions.skill: Using a third variable to improve a model
questions.stem: For practice hours $x$, the line for juniors is $y = 3x + 20$ and the line for seniors is $y = 3x + 30$. When $x = 10$, how many points higher is the seniors' prediction than the juniors' prediction?
questions.solution: Juniors: 3(10) + 20 = 50. Seniors: 3(10) + 30 = 60. The difference is 10 points.

questions.skill: Recognizing a third (lurking) variable
questions.stem: Fires attended by more firefighters tend to cause more damage. Which third variable best explains this?
choices: The age of the firefighters
The name of the fire station
The color of the fire trucks
The size of the fire
questions.answer: The size of the fire
questions.solution: A big fire both needs many firefighters and causes much damage. The firefighters are not causing the damage.

solve.answer: The size of the fire
solve.work: Bigger fires draw more firefighters and cause more damage.

questions.skill: Recognizing a third (lurking) variable
questions.stem: A variable that is not one of the two being compared but affects both of them is often called what?
choices: A prediction residual
A lurking variable
An outlier point
A random sample
questions.answer: A lurking variable
questions.solution: A hidden variable that influences both quantities being compared is called a lurking (or confounding) variable.

solve.answer: A lurking variable

questions.skill: Recognizing a third (lurking) variable
questions.stem: Which relationship is most likely explained by a third variable, rather than one quantity directly changing the other?
choices: Number of sheets in a stack of paper and the height of the stack
Number of tickets bought and the total cost of those tickets
Daily ice cream sales and daily numbers of people swimming
Miles driven and gallons of gas used on one trip
questions.answer: Daily ice cream sales and daily numbers of people swimming
questions.solution: Hot weather raises both ice cream sales and swimming. In the other pairs, one quantity directly changes the other.

solve.answer: Daily ice cream sales and daily numbers of people swimming
solve.work: Ice cream sales and swimming are both driven by hot weather; the others are direct relationships.

questions.skill: Recognizing a third (lurking) variable
questions.stem: Cities with more libraries also have more crime. Which third variable most likely explains this?
choices: The names of the mayors of those cities
The colors of the library buildings
The number of books on each library shelf
The number of people in the city
questions.answer: The number of people in the city
questions.solution: Larger cities tend to have both more libraries and more crime, simply because more people live there.

solve.answer: The number of people in the city
solve.work: Population size drives both library count and crime count.

questions.skill: Recognizing a third (lurking) variable
questions.stem: Towns where more bicycle helmets are sold also report more bicycle injuries. Which third variable most likely affects both of these?
choices: The brand name printed on the helmets
The average price of one helmet
The number of people who ride bikes
The color most helmets are painted
questions.answer: The number of people who ride bikes
questions.solution: A town with more bike riders sells more helmets and also has more injuries, so the number of riders affects both. The brand, the price and the color of helmets do not explain why injuries would rise along with sales.

solve.answer: The number of people who ride bikes
solve.work: More riders means more helmets bought and more injuries; the number of riders drives both. Color, brand and price do not plausibly drive injuries.

questions.skill: Splitting data by a third variable
questions.stem: A survey of 90 students records each student's grade and whether the student owns a bike. There are 60 ninth graders and 30 tenth graders. In all, 51 of the 90 students own a bike, and 39 of them are ninth graders. What percent of the tenth graders own a bike?
questions.solution: Split the students by grade. Bike owners who are tenth graders: 51 - 39 = 12. There are 30 tenth graders, so 12 / 30 = 0.4, which is 40 percent.

solve.work: Bike owners 51, of whom 39 are ninth graders, so 51 - 39 = 12 tenth graders own a bike. 12/30 = 0.4 = 40%.

questions.skill: Using a third variable to improve a model
questions.stem: A scatter plot shows plant height against days of growth. Plants grown in sun are drawn as blue dots and plants grown in shade as red dots. What does the color of a dot show?
choices: The light the plant grew in
The number of days it has grown
The height the plant has reached
The amount of water it received
questions.answer: The light the plant grew in
questions.solution: Height and days of growth are already shown by where the dot sits. The color adds a third variable, the kind of light (sun or shade), so a separate pattern can be seen for each group.

solve.answer: The light the plant grew in
solve.work: Blue = sun, red = shade, so color encodes the light condition (the third variable). Height and days are the axes; water is not shown.

questions.skill: Judging a source's credibility
questions.stem: A company says its Study Plus app raises grades, and it shows a chart as proof. Which question would best help you decide whether to believe the claim?
choices: What colors does the app's logo use?
Who chose the students in the data?
How many people have downloaded the app?
Does the app cost money to download?
questions.answer: Who chose the students in the data?
questions.solution: Whether a claim can be trusted depends on how the data were collected. If the company picked only its best students, the chart is misleading. The logo, the number of downloads and the cost say nothing about whether the grades really improved.

solve.answer: Who chose the students in the data?
solve.work: Credibility of the evidence depends on how the sample was chosen (selection bias). Logo colors, price and download counts do not test whether the chart supports the claim.

questions.skill: Using a third variable to improve a model
questions.stem: Basketball players are split by a third variable, position. For guards, the line that predicts free throws made in a drill is $f = 4w + 10$, and for centers it is $f = 2w + 10$, where $w$ is the number of weeks of practice. After 6 weeks, how many more free throws does the line predict for a guard than for a center?
questions.solution: Guard at 6 weeks: $4(6) + 10 = 34$. Center at 6 weeks: $2(6) + 10 = 22$. The difference is 34 - 22 = 12 free throws.

solve.issues: Soft spot: mostly tests evaluating two linear models; the third-variable idea is only framing.

questions.skill: Choose the variables that answer a question
questions.stem: Sara wants to know whether students who sleep more tend to score higher on quizzes. For each classmate she records hours of sleep, quiz score, shoe size and favorite color. Which two variables should she compare?
choices: Shoe size and favorite color
Hours of sleep and shoe size
Hours of sleep and quiz score
Quiz score and favorite color
questions.answer: Hours of sleep and quiz score
questions.solution: Her question is about sleep and quiz scores, so those are the two variables that matter. Shoe size and favorite color have nothing to do with her question, so pairs that include them would not help her answer it.

solve.answer: Hours of sleep and quiz score
solve.work: The question is whether more sleep goes with higher quiz scores, so the relevant variables are hours of sleep (explanatory) and quiz score (response). Shoe size and favorite color are irrelevant.

questions.skill: Recognizing a third variable
questions.stem: A dataset shows that students who own more books tend to have higher reading scores. A researcher thinks a student's age may affect both the number of books and the reading score. In this situation, how is age best described?
choices: The only cause of the higher reading scores
A variable that can be ignored because it was not in the question
A third variable that may influence both of the others
A sign that the data were collected incorrectly
questions.answer: A third variable that may influence both of the others
questions.solution: Older students may own more books and also read better. Age is then a third variable related to both, and it can help explain the pattern. It should not be ignored, and it does not mean the data are wrong.

solve.answer: A third variable that may influence both of the others
solve.work: Age may influence both books owned and reading score: a third (lurking/confounding) variable.

questions.skill: Comparing two groups
questions.stem: Of 50 students who used a study app, 35 passed the test. Of 50 students who did not use the app, 30 passed. How many percentage points higher is the pass percent of the app group than the pass percent of the other group?
questions.solution: App group: $\frac{35}{50} = 70$ percent. Other group: $\frac{30}{50} = 60$ percent. The difference is $70 - 60 = 10$ percentage points.

solve.work: App group 35/50 = 70 percent; other group 30/50 = 60 percent. Difference = 10 percentage points.

questions.skill: Doubting a claim about data
questions.stem: A website says, "Our vitamin drink raises math scores by 30 percent!" Which detail would make you the MOST doubtful of the claim?
choices: The website sells the drink and does not say how scores were measured
The study included a comparison group that did not drink it
The study reports how many students took part
The data were collected by an outside research team
questions.answer: The website sells the drink and does not say how scores were measured
questions.solution: A seller with something to gain, and no information on how the scores were measured, is a reason to doubt. A comparison group, a stated number of students and independent researchers all make a claim more credible.

solve.answer: The website sells the drink and does not say how scores were measured
solve.work: A seller with an interest in the result who gives no measurement method is the most reason for doubt; the other details make the claim more credible.

questions.skill: Judging the credibility of a data source
questions.stem: A tutoring company's ad shows the quiz scores of its five best students and says, "Our students improve fast!" What is the main problem with this data?
choices: It shows only the best results, not a typical group of students
Quiz scores cannot be used to measure learning at all
Showing five students gives too much data to understand
The company should have shown even fewer students
questions.answer: It shows only the best results, not a typical group of students
questions.solution: Choosing only the top students hides the rest. A fair claim needs results from a typical or random group.

solve.answer: It shows only the best results, not a typical group of students
solve.work: Cherry-picked best five students are not typical.

questions.skill: Judging the credibility of a data source
questions.stem: Two sources give the population of a town. Source 1 is a national census that counted every household two years ago. Source 2 is an undated blog post that gives a different number and no explanation. Which should you use, and why?
choices: Source 2, because a blog post is bound to be newer than a national census
Source 1, because its method is clear and it comes from a full count
Source 2, because a different number shows more careful work
Source 1, because official sources are always exactly right
questions.answer: Source 1, because its method is clear and it comes from a full count
questions.solution: Source 1 explains how the number was found and is dated. Source 2 has no date or explanation. Even official sources are not perfect, but this one is much more credible.

solve.answer: Source 1, because its method is clear and it comes from a full count
solve.work: Census is a full count with a clear method; blog is undated and unexplained. 'Always exactly right' overclaims.

questions.skill: Judging the credibility of a data source
questions.stem: A graph in an advertisement has a vertical axis that starts at 96 instead of 0. The bars show 97 for last year and 99 for this year, and the second bar looks several times taller. What is the problem?
choices: Bars should always be drawn in order from tallest to shortest
Values of 97 and 99 are too close together to be graphed at all
Starting the axis at 96 makes a small change look very large
A vertical axis must always count up by tens or hundreds
questions.answer: Starting the axis at 96 makes a small change look very large
questions.solution: Because the axis does not start at 0, the difference of 2 looks huge. A misleading scale is a reason to doubt how data are presented.

solve.answer: Starting the axis at 96 makes a small change look very large
solve.work: Truncated axis: 97 vs 99 drawn as 1 vs 3 units above 96, exaggerating a small change.

questions.skill: Judging the credibility of a data source
questions.stem: A poll reports that 54 percent of people favor a new park, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. According to the poll, what is the lowest percent that the true value could reasonably be?
questions.solution: The true value is likely within 3 percentage points of 54 percent, so the lowest reasonable value is 54 - 3 = 51 percent.

questions.skill: Judging the credibility of a data source
questions.stem: A study says a candy does not cause cavities. The candy's maker paid for the study, and only the maker has seen the full data. Which question is the most useful to ask first?
choices: Does the candy come in more than one flavor, shape or size?
Is the maker's name printed clearly on the front of the report?
How many people at the company really enjoy eating this candy?
Can independent researchers check the data and methods?
questions.answer: Can independent researchers check the data and methods?
questions.solution: Because the maker paid for the study and holds the data, the key issue is whether others can check how the data were collected and analyzed.

solve.answer: Can independent researchers check the data and methods?
solve.work: Funding bias plus hidden data: first ask whether independent researchers can verify.

questions.skill: Choosing relevant variables
questions.stem: Ben wants to predict a student's final exam score. His dataset has: homework average, shirt size, number of absences, locker number and hours of TV watched last year. Which pair of variables is the most reasonable to use?
choices: Shirt size and locker number
Homework average and number of absences
Locker number and hours of TV watched last year
Shirt size and hours of TV watched
questions.answer: Homework average and number of absences
questions.solution: Homework average and absences relate to how the student is doing in the course. Shirt size and locker number have no reasonable link to an exam score.

solve.answer: Homework average and number of absences
solve.work: Homework average and absences plausibly relate to exam score; shirt size, locker number irrelevant; last year's TV weak.

questions.skill: Choosing relevant variables
questions.stem: Rosa wants to study how study hours and sleep hours together relate to test score. Her table has these columns: study hours, sleep hours, test score, hair color and number of siblings. How many of the columns will she use?
questions.solution: She uses study hours, sleep hours and test score. Hair color and number of siblings are not part of her question. That is 3 columns.

solve.work: Study hours, sleep hours, test score = 3 columns.

questions.skill: Choosing relevant variables
questions.stem: A dataset records each person's height in inches and also in centimeters. Why is it not helpful to use both as predictors of weight?
choices: Height cannot help predict a person's weight in any situation
Centimeters are always less accurate than inches for people
They give the same information, so the second adds nothing
Two predictors that have units can never be used together
questions.answer: They give the same information, so the second adds nothing
questions.solution: Inches and centimeters are the same measurement in two units, so using both is redundant.

solve.answer: They give the same information, so the second adds nothing
solve.work: Inches and centimeters are the same measurement rescaled; redundant.

questions.skill: Choosing relevant variables
questions.stem: A school wants to predict, before the semester starts, whether a student will pass a course. Which variable could NOT be used for this?
choices: The student's grade in the previous math course
The student's attendance last year
The student's score on a placement quiz
The student's final course grade
questions.answer: The student's final course grade
questions.solution: The final grade is not known before the semester starts, so it cannot be used to predict the result.

solve.answer: The student's final course grade
solve.work: Final course grade is not known before the semester starts (and is essentially the outcome).

questions.skill: Choosing relevant variables
questions.stem: A dataset has 5 numeric variables. A student plans to make one scatter plot for every different pair of variables. How many scatter plots will she make?
questions.solution: Each variable can be paired with 4 others, which gives 5 x 4 = 20 ordered pairs. A plot of x against y shows the same pair as y against x, so divide by 2: 10 plots.

questions.skill: Evaluating a dataset for a question
questions.stem: To estimate how many hours a night teens in North Carolina sleep, a researcher surveys only the members of one school's early-morning swim team. What is the main concern?
choices: Sleep is much too hard to measure accurately for any teens
A swim team has far too many members for her to ever survey
The researcher should have surveyed adults instead of teens
The swim team may not be typical of teens in the state
questions.answer: The swim team may not be typical of teens in the state
questions.solution: The sample comes from one unusual group, so it may not represent all teens.

solve.answer: The swim team may not be typical of teens in the state
solve.work: Early-morning swimmers are not representative of NC teens' sleep.

questions.skill: Evaluating a dataset for a question
questions.stem: A dataset has 250 rows. The income is missing in 20 percent of the rows. How many rows have an income value?
questions.solution: 20 percent of 250 is 50 rows missing. 250 - 50 = 200 rows have an income.

questions.skill: Evaluating a dataset for a question
questions.stem: Alex wants to know whether summers in his town are getting warmer. He has the daily highs for June, July and August from 1950 to 1960 only. What is wrong with using this data?
choices: It stops in 1960, so it says nothing about recent summers
Summer temperatures cannot be compared across years
Daily highs are not related to the weather in any way
Ten years of data is always far too much data to examine
questions.answer: It stops in 1960, so it says nothing about recent summers
questions.solution: To tell whether summers are getting warmer now, he needs data from recent years as well.

solve.answer: It stops in 1960, so it says nothing about recent summers
solve.work: Data from 1950-1960 only cannot show a trend into the present.

questions.skill: Evaluating a dataset for a question
questions.stem: A dataset has 130 rows. There are 18 rows missing the weight and 7 rows missing the height, and no row is missing both. A student deletes every row that is missing a value. How many rows are left?
questions.solution: No row is counted twice, so 18 + 7 = 25 rows are deleted. 130 - 25 = 105 rows remain.

questions.skill: Evaluating a dataset for a question
questions.stem: A table has the columns city, population and average monthly rent. Which question can these data help answer?
choices: Do people in larger cities tend to have more free time?
Do cities with more people tend to have higher rents?
Which of the cities has the best public parks in it?
Do families with more children pay lower rents?
questions.answer: Do cities with more people tend to have higher rents?
questions.solution: Only the first question uses the variables in the table, population and rent.

solve.answer: Do cities with more people tend to have higher rents?
solve.work: Only population and rent are available per city: question 2.

questions.skill: Splitting data by a third variable
questions.stem: Greenhouse 1 has 15 tomato plants with a mean height of 80 centimeters. Greenhouse 2 has 25 tomato plants with a mean height of 88 centimeters. What is the mean height of all 40 plants, in centimeters?
questions.solution: Total heights: 15 x 80 = 1,200 and 25 x 88 = 2,200, together 3,400. Divide by 40 plants: 85 centimeters.

questions.skill: Splitting data by a third variable
questions.stem: Among 40 ninth graders, 28 passed a test. Among 60 tenth graders, 51 passed. By how many percentage points does the pass rate of the tenth graders exceed that of the ninth graders?
questions.solution: Ninth graders: 28 / 40 = 70 percent. Tenth graders: 51 / 60 = 85 percent. The difference is 85 - 70 = 15 percentage points.

questions.skill: Splitting data by a third variable
questions.stem: In a dataset, the 12 boys have a mean score of 75 and the 18 girls have a mean score of 75. What is the mean score of all 30 students?
questions.solution: The total is 12 x 75 + 18 x 75 = 900 + 1,350 = 2,250. Divide by 30: 75. If both groups have the same mean, the combined mean is the same.

solve.work: Both groups mean 75, so combined mean 75.

questions.skill: Splitting data by a third variable
questions.stem: A shop surveyed 200 customers: 120 adults and 80 teens. Thirty percent of the adults and 60 percent of the teens bought a pass. How many of the 200 customers bought a pass?
questions.solution: Adults: 30 percent of 120 is 36. Teens: 60 percent of 80 is 48. Together 36 + 48 = 84 customers.

questions.skill: Splitting data by a third variable
questions.stem: Why might an analyst split a dataset by a third variable before comparing two groups?
choices: Splitting always forces the two groups to have exactly equal averages
A third variable is needed so that the dataset becomes much larger
Groups may be compared only after the data are cut into three parts
The groups may differ in a third variable that affects results
questions.answer: The groups may differ in a third variable that affects results
questions.solution: If the groups differ in the third variable, a difference between them may come from that variable. Comparing within each level of it gives a fairer picture.

solve.answer: The groups may differ in a third variable that affects results
solve.work: Splitting controls for a third variable on which the groups may differ (confounding).

questions.skill: Using a third variable to improve a model
questions.stem: After splitting by drink type, cooling is modeled as tea: $T = 90 - 3m$ and coffee: $T = 95 - 4m$, where $T$ is the temperature in degrees and $m$ is the minutes. What temperature does the coffee line predict after 10 minutes?
questions.solution: Use the coffee line: $T = 95 - 4(10) = 55$ degrees.

questions.skill: Using a third variable to improve a model
questions.stem: A single line is fit to the data for all students. Its residuals are mostly positive for the morning class and mostly negative for the evening class. What does this suggest?
choices: Class period matters, so the groups need separate lines
The line is perfect and no change is needed
The evening students should be deleted from the data
The morning scores should be lowered to fit the line
questions.answer: Class period matters, so the groups need separate lines
questions.solution: A pattern in the residuals that follows a group shows that the group variable should be used in the model.

solve.answer: Class period matters, so the groups need separate lines
solve.work: Systematic residuals by class mean class period is a missing variable: fit separate lines.

questions.skill: Using a third variable to improve a model
questions.stem: After splitting by sport, the best-fit lines for height $h$ (in inches) and age $a$ (in years) are: swimmers, $h = 2a + 30$; runners, $h = 3a + 18$. At what age do the two lines predict the same height?
questions.solution: Set the heights equal: $2a + 30 = 3a + 18$. Subtract $2a$ and 18 from both sides: $12 = a$. So the age is 12.

solve.issues: Context is a little odd (linear height-by-age lines for athletes) but the math is clean.

questions.skill: Using a third variable to improve a model
questions.stem: A scatter plot of fuel used against distance for all vehicles shows two separate, nearly straight bands of points. What would be most helpful for improving the model?
choices: Draw one line through the middle of the gap between the bands
Find a variable that separates the bands and fit a line to each
Delete the points of whichever band has the fewer points in it, then refit
Use one much flatter line that lies in between the two bands
questions.answer: Find a variable that separates the bands and fit a line to each
questions.solution: Two straight bands suggest two groups. A variable that identifies the groups allows a separate line for each.

solve.answer: Find a variable that separates the bands and fit a line to each
solve.work: Two bands suggest a grouping variable (e.g., vehicle type); separate and fit a line to each.

questions.skill: Using a third variable to improve a model
questions.stem: The line for the morning class is $y = 4x + 50$, where $x$ is hours studied. How many hours of study does the line predict for a score of 78?
questions.solution: Solve $4x + 50 = 78$: $4x = 28$, so $x = 7$ hours.

questions.skill: Recognizing a third (lurking) variable
questions.stem: Students who eat breakfast at school have higher attendance. Which could be a third variable that influences both?
choices: How steady the student's morning routine is at home
The color of the trays in the cafeteria line
The number of lockers in the school hallway
The name of the school's sports team mascot
questions.answer: How steady the student's morning routine is at home
questions.solution: A family's morning routines could affect both whether a child eats breakfast at school and whether the child arrives on time and attends.

solve.answer: How steady the student's morning routine is at home
solve.work: A steady morning routine could lead to both eating school breakfast and attending; others irrelevant.

questions.skill: Recognizing a third (lurking) variable
questions.stem: Researchers want to compare reading scores of students who visit the library often with those who do not, while accounting for age. Which approach best accounts for age?
choices: Compare only the oldest visitors with only the youngest non-visitors
Compare frequent visitors and non-visitors within each age group
Ignore age and compare all visitors with all non-visitors
Compare students' reading scores to their shoe sizes
questions.answer: Compare frequent visitors and non-visitors within each age group
questions.solution: Comparing within each age group keeps age the same in each comparison.

solve.answer: Compare frequent visitors and non-visitors within each age group
solve.work: Stratify by age: compare within each age group.

questions.skill: Recognizing a third (lurking) variable
questions.stem: Counties that sold more air conditioners also have more heat-related hospital visits. A reporter writes that air conditioners cause the hospital visits. What is the best response?
choices: The claim is right, because the two go up together
Hospital visits cause people to go out and buy air conditioners
Hot weather may be behind both the sales and the visits
Counties cannot be compared with each other in this way at all
questions.answer: Hot weather may be behind both the sales and the visits
questions.solution: Hot weather would raise both air conditioner sales and heat-related illness, so the link does not show that one causes the other.

solve.answer: Hot weather may be behind both the sales and the visits
solve.work: Hot weather drives both AC sales and heat-related visits.

questions.skill: Recognizing a third (lurking) variable
questions.stem: Over 200 days, 120 were hot days. High ice cream sales happened on 96 of the hot days and on 8 of the days that were not hot. What percent of the days that were not hot had high sales?
questions.solution: Days that were not hot: 200 - 120 = 80. High sales on 8 of them: 8 / 80 = 10 percent. (On hot days it was 96 / 120 = 80 percent: the weather is the third variable.)

questions.skill: Recognizing a third (lurking) variable
questions.stem: Across 50 towns, the correlation between umbrella sales and rainy-day car accidents is $r = 0.9$. Among towns with about the same rainfall, umbrella sales and accidents show no link. What does this suggest?
choices: Umbrella sales cause the accidents in each of these towns
The accidents cause umbrella sales in each of these towns
The correlation of 0.9 must be a mistake in calculation
Rainfall is a third variable that explains the link
questions.answer: Rainfall is a third variable that explains the link
questions.solution: When the link disappears among towns with the same rainfall, rainfall is behind both umbrella sales and accidents.

solve.answer: Rainfall is a third variable that explains the link
solve.work: Link disappears when rainfall is held fixed: rainfall is the confounder.

questions.skill: Splitting data by a third variable
questions.stem: Two tutoring programs report results. Program X had 80 beginners, 48 of whom passed, and 20 advanced students, 19 of whom passed. Program Y had 20 beginners, 10 of whom passed, and 80 advanced students, 70 of whom passed. Program X has the higher pass rate at each level, yet Program Y has the higher pass rate overall. Which statement best explains this?
choices: Program Y must have recorded its results incorrectly
Program X is actually worse than Program Y at every level
Program X had a much larger share of beginners, who pass less often in both programs
Percentages from small groups should always be ignored
questions.answer: Program X had a much larger share of beginners, who pass less often in both programs
questions.solution: Beginners: X passed $\frac{48}{80} = 60$ percent, Y passed $\frac{10}{20} = 50$ percent. Advanced: X passed $\frac{19}{20} = 95$ percent, Y passed $\frac{70}{80} = 87.5$ percent. So X is higher at both levels. Overall, X passed $\frac{67}{100}$ and Y passed $\frac{80}{100}$. Most of X's students were beginners, who pass less often in either program, which pulls X's overall rate down.

solve.answer: Program X had a much larger share of beginners, who pass less often in both programs
solve.work: X: beginners 48/80 = 60, advanced 19/20 = 95, overall 67/100 = 67 percent. Y: beginners 10/20 = 50, advanced 70/80 = 87.5, overall 80/100 = 80 percent. X wins in each level, Y overall (Simpson's paradox) because X has 80 percent beginners, who pass less often in both programs.

questions.skill: Combining group means
questions.stem: In a dataset, 20 students in group A have a mean quiz score of 70, and 30 students in group B have a mean quiz score of 90. What is the mean quiz score of all 50 students?
questions.solution: Total points in group A: $20 \times 70 = 1{,}400$. Total points in group B: $30 \times 90 = 2{,}700$. All 50 students: $\frac{1{,}400 + 2{,}700}{50} = \frac{4{,}100}{50} = 82$.

questions.skill: Splitting data to improve a model
questions.stem: A student plots test score against hours studied for 60 students and finds only a weak pattern. She then separates the students into a morning class and an evening class. Each group shows a clear, steady pattern, but the two patterns are different. What does this suggest?
choices: Class time is a third variable that should be included in the analysis
Hours studied has no relationship with test score
The data should be thrown away because the first pattern was weak
Evening students are better at math than morning students
questions.answer: Class time is a third variable that should be included in the analysis
questions.solution: The weak overall pattern comes from mixing two groups with different patterns. Splitting by class time reveals the relationship in each group, so class time should be part of the model.

solve.answer: Class time is a third variable that should be included in the analysis
solve.work: Splitting by class reveals clear but different patterns, so class time is a third variable that should be included. Hours studied clearly does relate within groups, so option 1 is wrong; option 4 is not supported.

questions.skill: Judging the credibility of a data source
questions.stem: A city wants to know what share of its teenagers ride a bike to school. Source 1: a voluntary online poll run by a bike store, with 9,000 responses. Source 2: a random sample of 600 teens chosen by a university, with its methods published. Source 3: an article saying "experts agree," with no numbers. Which source is the most credible?
choices: Source 2, because the sample was random and the methods are open
Source 1, because 9,000 responses is far more than 600 responses
Source 3, because experts know more about teens than a survey
Source 1, because a bike store knows the most about bike riders
questions.answer: Source 2, because the sample was random and the methods are open
questions.solution: A volunteer poll run by a seller is likely biased, however large. A random sample with published methods, even if smaller, is the most trustworthy. Source 3 gives no data.

solve.answer: Source 2, because the sample was random and the methods are open
solve.work: Random sample with published methods beats a large voluntary (self-selected, store-run) poll and an unsupported claim.

questions.skill: Judging the credibility of a data source
questions.stem: A survey was mailed to 2,000 households, and 250 households mailed it back. What percent of the households that received the survey returned it?
questions.solution: 250 out of 2,000 is 250 / 2,000 = 0.125, which is 12.5 percent. A low return rate is a reason to ask whether the answers represent everyone.

questions.skill: Judging the credibility of a data source
questions.stem: Which finding would most increase your trust in a reported study result?
choices: Many large news sites reported the result on the very same day
A second team, using a new group of people, found a similar result
The author of the study says that she is completely sure it is right
The result is simple enough that anyone can explain it to a friend
questions.answer: A second team, using a new group of people, found a similar result
questions.solution: Results that can be repeated by independent researchers on new data are more credible. Publicity, confidence and simplicity do not test a result.

solve.answer: A second team, using a new group of people, found a similar result
solve.work: Independent replication with a new sample increases trust most.

questions.skill: Judging the credibility of a data source
questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a good reason to doubt a data source?
choices: The sample was made up of people who chose to volunteer to answer online
The authors will earn money if the data happen to support their claim
The data were collected by a university and checked by reviewers
The report does not say how many people were asked
questions.answer: The data were collected by a university and checked by reviewers
questions.solution: Careful collection and independent review are reasons to trust data. A volunteer sample, a financial interest and missing information about sample size are reasons to doubt it.

solve.answer: The data were collected by a university and checked by reviewers
solve.work: University collection with review is a reason for trust, not doubt; the others are real red flags.

questions.skill: Judging the credibility of a data source
questions.stem: A poll finds that 52 percent of voters prefer Candidate A and 48 percent prefer Candidate B, with a margin of error of 4 percentage points. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Candidate A is certainly ahead because 52 is more than 48
Candidate B is certainly ahead because the margin lowers A's number
The poll is useless because every poll has some margin of error
The race is too close for this poll to say who is ahead
questions.answer: The race is too close for this poll to say who is ahead
questions.solution: A's support could be 48 to 56 percent and B's 44 to 52 percent, so the ranges overlap. The poll cannot show who leads, though it is still useful information.

solve.answer: The race is too close for this poll to say who is ahead
solve.work: A: 48-56, B: 44-52; intervals overlap, so the poll cannot say who leads.

questions.skill: Choosing relevant variables
questions.stem: To study whether exercise lowers blood pressure in adults, researchers record exercise minutes, blood pressure, age and diet. Why would they include age?
choices: Age may affect both exercise and blood pressure levels in adults
Age is the variable being predicted in the study
Every study must record a person's age and nothing else
More columns always make the conclusions more accurate
questions.answer: Age may affect both exercise and blood pressure levels in adults
questions.solution: A variable that may influence both exercise and blood pressure can distort the comparison, so researchers record it and take it into account.

solve.answer: Age may affect both exercise and blood pressure levels in adults
solve.work: Age is a possible confounder affecting both exercise and blood pressure.

questions.skill: Choosing relevant variables
questions.stem: To compare how safe the roads are in two cities of very different sizes, which variable is the better choice?
choices: Total accidents in each city
Accidents per 10,000 residents
Total residents in each city
Total number of roads in each city
questions.answer: Accidents per 10,000 residents
questions.solution: Counts depend on the size of the city. A rate such as accidents per 10,000 residents makes the cities comparable.

solve.answer: Accidents per 10,000 residents
solve.work: A rate per population adjusts for city size.

questions.skill: Choosing relevant variables
questions.stem: City A had 90 accidents and has 30,000 residents. City B had 60 accidents and has 12,000 residents. How many more accidents per 10,000 residents does City B have than City A?
questions.solution: City A: 90 / 3 = 30 accidents per 10,000 residents (30,000 residents is three groups of 10,000). City B: 60 / 1.2 = 50 per 10,000. The difference is 50 - 30 = 20.

questions.skill: Choosing relevant variables
questions.stem: Four variables are checked against a final score. The correlation coefficients are: hours studied, $r = 0.71$; absences, $r = -0.64$; shoe size, $r = 0.03$; homework average, $r = 0.82$. Which two variables are the strongest predictors of the final score?
choices: Hours studied and number of absences
Homework average and student shoe size
Homework average and hours studied
Absences and shoe size
questions.answer: Homework average and hours studied
questions.solution: Strength depends on how far $r$ is from 0, not on its sign. The two largest values of |r| are 0.82 (homework average) and 0.71 (hours studied).

solve.answer: Homework average and hours studied
solve.work: |r|: homework 0.82, hours 0.71, absences 0.64, shoe 0.03. Top two: homework, hours.

questions.skill: Choosing relevant variables
questions.stem: A model predicts a house's price from its floor area, but its errors are large. The residuals are mostly positive for houses near the lake and mostly negative for houses far from the lake. Which variable should be added?
choices: Color of the front door
First name of the owner
Number of letters in the street name
Distance from the lake
questions.answer: Distance from the lake
questions.solution: The errors follow a pattern tied to location near the lake, so the distance from the lake is the variable that can improve the model.

solve.answer: Distance from the lake
solve.work: Residual pattern by lake proximity means distance from lake explains the missing variation.

questions.skill: Evaluating a dataset for a question
questions.stem: The hours of sleep recorded for 8 students are 7, 9, 8, 6, 70, 8, 7 and 8. The value 70 was a typing mistake for 7. What is the correct mean number of hours of sleep?
questions.solution: Correct the value: 7, 9, 8, 6, 7, 8, 7, 8. The sum is 60, and 60 / 8 = 7.5 hours.

questions.skill: Evaluating a dataset for a question
questions.stem: Each of 60 survey forms has 10 questions. Across all of the forms, 90 answers are blank. What percent of all the answers are blank?
questions.solution: There are 60 x 10 = 600 answers in all. 90 / 600 = 0.15, which is 15 percent.

questions.skill: Evaluating a dataset for a question
questions.stem: A student plots reading score against hours of screen time for 30 students. The three highest reading scores are all missing a screen-time value, so she deletes those three rows. Why could this mislead her?
choices: Deleting rows with missing values always makes the pattern stronger
Thirty students are too few to make any kind of plot
The deleted students may be unlike the others in the data
Rows with missing values must always be kept in the data as zeros
questions.answer: The deleted students may be unlike the others in the data
questions.solution: The missing rows are not random: they are the top scorers. Removing them can change the pattern that the plot shows.

solve.answer: The deleted students may be unlike the others in the data
solve.work: Removing the top scorers non-randomly can bias the pattern; they may differ from the rest.

questions.skill: Evaluating a dataset for a question
questions.stem: To estimate the average cost of a school lunch across North Carolina, which dataset is better?
choices: Prices from all 12 of the schools in one small mountain town
Prices from the 3 most expensive schools in the whole state
Prices from 15 schools picked at random in a different state
Prices from 15 schools picked at random around the state
questions.answer: Prices from 15 schools picked at random around the state
questions.solution: A random choice of schools from across the state represents the state. One town, only the highest prices, or a different state do not.

solve.answer: Prices from 15 schools picked at random around the state
solve.work: Random schools across NC represent the state; others are local, extreme or wrong state.

questions.skill: Evaluating a dataset for a question
questions.stem: A dataset about a town pool lists daily visitors, but only for June and July. A student uses it to claim the pool has about the same number of visitors every day of the year. Which statement is true?
choices: Two summer months cannot support a claim about the entire year
A pool's visitor counts are the wrong kind of data to use
Daily counts can never be used to make a claim about weeks
Any two months of data are enough to describe a whole year
questions.answer: Two summer months cannot support a claim about the entire year
questions.solution: The data cover only the summer, and winter attendance could be very different, so the claim about the whole year is not supported.

solve.answer: Two summer months cannot support a claim about the entire year
solve.work: Summer-only data cannot support a whole-year claim.

questions.skill: Splitting data by a third variable
questions.stem: A clinic compared two medicines. Medicine P: 90 mild cases, of which 81 recovered, and 10 severe cases, of which 3 recovered. Medicine Q: 10 mild cases, of which 10 recovered, and 90 severe cases, of which 54 recovered. Which statement is true?
choices: Q is higher for each severity, but P is higher overall
P is higher for each severity and also higher overall
Q is higher for each severity and also higher overall
P is higher for severe cases, but Q is higher overall
questions.answer: Q is higher for each severity, but P is higher overall
questions.solution: Mild: P 81/90 = 90 percent, Q 10/10 = 100 percent. Severe: P 3/10 = 30 percent, Q 54/90 = 60 percent. Overall: P 84/100 = 84 percent, Q 64/100 = 64 percent. Most of P's patients were mild cases, which recover more often.

solve.answer: Q is higher for each severity, but P is higher overall
solve.work: Mild: P 81/90 = 90%, Q 10/10 = 100%. Severe: P 3/10 = 30%, Q 54/90 = 60%. Overall: P 84/100 = 84%, Q 64/100 = 64%. Q higher in each, P higher overall (Simpson's paradox).

questions.skill: Splitting data by a third variable
questions.stem: The mean score of 50 students is 84. The 20 students in group 1 have a mean score of 75. What is the mean score of the 30 students in group 2?
questions.solution: Total points: 50 x 84 = 4,200. Group 1 earned 20 x 75 = 1,500. Group 2 earned 4,200 - 1,500 = 2,700, so its mean is 2,700 / 30 = 90.

questions.skill: Splitting data by a third variable
questions.stem: Of 80 students, 30 are juniors and 50 are seniors. Overall, 70 percent of the 80 students passed, and 60 percent of the juniors passed. What percent of the seniors passed?
questions.solution: Passed overall: 56. Passed among juniors: 18. So 56 - 18 = 38 seniors passed, and 38 / 50 = 76 percent.

questions.skill: Splitting data by a third variable
questions.stem: A dataset is split into three groups. Group 1 has 10 students with a mean of 60, group 2 has 20 students with a mean of 70, and group 3 has 20 students with a mean of 85. What is the mean of all 50 students?
questions.solution: Totals: 600 + 1,400 + 1,700 = 3,700. Divide by 50 students: 74.

questions.skill: Splitting data by a third variable
questions.stem: A researcher finds that athletes sleep 7.2 hours a night on average and non-athletes sleep 8.1 hours. She suspects that age is responsible for the difference. Which step would best check this?
choices: Compare the oldest athletes with the youngest non-athletes
Compare athletes and non-athletes within each age group
Average the two sleep times into a single number
Remove all students younger than the athletes
questions.answer: Compare athletes and non-athletes within each age group
questions.solution: To see whether age explains the gap, hold age fixed by comparing the two groups among students of the same age.

solve.answer: Compare athletes and non-athletes within each age group
solve.work: Control for age by comparing within each age group.

questions.skill: Using a third variable to improve a model
questions.stem: In the evening class, one student who studied 2 hours scored 58, and another who studied 6 hours scored 82. Using the line through these two points, what score does it predict for a student who studied 5 hours?
questions.solution: Slope = (82 - 58) / (6 - 2) = 6 points per hour. From 2 hours to 5 hours is 3 more hours, so the score is 58 + 6 x 3 = 76.

questions.skill: Using a third variable to improve a model
questions.stem: Group X's line has slope 3 and passes through the point $(4, 25)$. What value does the line predict when $x = 0$?
questions.solution: Going from $x = 4$ back to $x = 0$ is 4 steps of 3 down: 25 - 12 = 13.

questions.skill: Using a third variable to improve a model
questions.stem: Across all employees of a company, salary seems to go down as years of experience go up. Within each of the two departments, though, salary goes up with experience. Which explanation fits?
choices: Experience actually lowers salary in both of the departments
The departments' data must have been recorded incorrectly
One department pays far more, and its staff are newer
Salary and experience are not related at all
questions.answer: One department pays far more, and its staff are newer
questions.solution: If the higher-paying department has mostly newer staff, the combined data can slope downward even though each department slopes upward. Department is the third variable.

solve.answer: One department pays far more, and its staff are newer
solve.work: If the high-paying department has mostly low-experience staff, pooling yields an overall negative trend while each department is positive (Simpson's paradox).

questions.skill: Using a third variable to improve a model
questions.stem: The line for the morning class is $y = 4x + 50$. A morning-class student studied 3 hours and scored 71. What is the residual (actual score minus predicted score)?
questions.solution: Predicted: 4(3) + 50 = 62. Residual = 71 - 62 = 9.

questions.skill: Using a third variable to improve a model
questions.stem: One line fit to all students is $y = 2.5x + 48$, while the line for the morning class alone is $y = 4x + 50$. For a morning-class student who studied 6 hours, how many points higher is the prediction from the morning line than from the line for all students?
questions.solution: Morning line: 4(6) + 50 = 74. All-students line: 2.5(6) + 48 = 63. The difference is 74 - 63 = 11 points.

questions.skill: Recognizing a third (lurking) variable
questions.stem: Over 300 days, 40 percent were hot. High ice cream sales happened on 75 percent of the hot days. Overall, 99 of the 300 days had high sales. What percent of the days that were not hot had high sales?
questions.solution: Hot days: 120, with 75 percent high: 90 days. So 99 - 90 = 9 high-sales days came from the 180 days that were not hot. 9 / 180 = 5 percent.

questions.skill: Recognizing a third (lurking) variable
questions.stem: Students who spend more hours on homework tend to have lower grades. Which third variable could explain this without homework hurting grades?
choices: How hard the student's courses are overall
How tall the student is for his age
How many pencils the student owns
The color of the student's backpack
questions.answer: How hard the student's courses are overall
questions.solution: Harder courses can mean both more homework hours and lower grades.

solve.answer: How hard the student's courses are overall
solve.work: Harder courses mean more homework time and lower grades.

questions.skill: Recognizing a third (lurking) variable
questions.stem: A school wants to know whether a tutoring program improves scores, while taking prior achievement into account. Which comparison is the best?
choices: Compare the tutored students' highest scores with the non-tutored students' lowest scores
Compare tutored and non-tutored students who started with similar prior scores
Compare all tutored students with all others, whatever their prior scores
Compare the tutored students' scores with the non-tutored students' ages
questions.answer: Compare tutored and non-tutored students who started with similar prior scores
questions.solution: Matching students on prior achievement keeps that variable from distorting the comparison.

solve.answer: Compare tutored and non-tutored students who started with similar prior scores
solve.work: Control prior achievement by comparing students with similar prior scores.

questions.skill: Recognizing a third (lurking) variable
questions.stem: Which finding would most strongly suggest that a third variable is NOT responsible for a link between X and Y?
choices: The third variable is strongly linked to both X and Y in the data
The third variable differs a lot between the high-X and the low-X groups
X and Y stay strongly linked within each level of the third variable
The link between X and Y vanishes within each level of the third variable
questions.answer: X and Y stay strongly linked within each level of the third variable
questions.solution: If the link remains when the third variable is held fixed, that variable cannot be the full explanation of the link.

solve.answer: X and Y stay strongly linked within each level of the third variable
solve.work: If the X-Y link persists within each level of the third variable, that variable is not explaining it.

questions.skill: Recognizing a third (lurking) variable
questions.stem: Over 200 days, 50 were hot and 150 were not. High ice cream sales happened on 80 percent of the hot days and on 20 percent of the days that were not hot. What percent of all 200 days had high sales?
questions.solution: Hot: 80 percent of 50 = 40 days. Not hot: 20 percent of 150 = 30 days. Total 70 days out of 200 = 35 percent.

questions.skill: Describing direction and form
questions.stem: A scatter plot has the points $(1, 2)$, $(2, 4)$, $(3, 5)$, $(4, 7)$ and $(5, 9)$. Which best describes the pattern?
choices: negative and roughly linear
no clear pattern
a curve that levels off
positive and roughly linear
questions.answer: positive and roughly linear
questions.solution: As $x$ increases, $y$ increases steadily by about 2 each time, so the points rise along a roughly straight line: a positive, roughly linear association.

solve.answer: positive and roughly linear
solve.work: y increases with x by 2,1,2,2: positive and close to a straight line.

questions.skill: Reading a point on a scatter plot
questions.stem: In a scatter plot, each point is (hours studied, quiz score). What does the point $(3, 78)$ mean?
choices: A student studied for 78 hours and scored 3
A student studied for 3 hours and scored 78
Three students each scored 78
A student scored 3 points higher after studying for 78 hours
questions.answer: A student studied for 3 hours and scored 78
questions.solution: The first number is the hours studied and the second is the quiz score, so the point is a student who studied 3 hours and scored 78.

solve.answer: A student studied for 3 hours and scored 78
solve.work: x = hours studied = 3, y = quiz score = 78: a student studied 3 hours and scored 78.

questions.skill: Predicting from a line of best fit
questions.stem: A line of best fit for hours studied ($x$) and quiz score ($y$) is $y = 4x + 50$. Use the line to predict the quiz score of a student who studies 6 hours.

questions.skill: Reading a point in context
questions.stem: A scatter plot shows each student's hours of sleep (horizontal) and the minutes needed to finish a puzzle (vertical). One student is plotted at $(8, 12)$. How many minutes did that student need to finish the puzzle?
questions.solution: In an ordered pair the first number is the horizontal value and the second is the vertical value. At $(8, 12)$ the vertical value is 12, so the student needed 12 minutes.

solve.work: Point (8, 12): x = 8 hours of sleep, y = 12 minutes for the puzzle.

questions.skill: Reading a point in context
questions.stem: Five dogs are plotted with age in years on the horizontal axis and weight in pounds on the vertical axis: $(1, 20)$, $(3, 45)$, $(5, 60)$, $(8, 58)$ and $(10, 50)$. What is the age, in years, of the heaviest dog?
questions.solution: The heaviest dog has the greatest vertical value, 60 pounds, at the point $(5, 60)$. The age is the horizontal value, 5 years.

solve.work: Largest weight is 60 at (5, 60), so the heaviest dog is 5 years old.

questions.skill: Reading a point in context
questions.stem: On a scatter plot, temperature in degrees is on the horizontal axis and the number of cups of cocoa sold is on the vertical axis. On one day it was 30 degrees and 25 cups were sold. Which ordered pair is plotted for that day?
questions.solution: The horizontal value (temperature) is written first and the vertical value (cups sold) second, so the point is $(30, 25)$.

questions.skill: Reading a point in context
questions.stem: Four students are plotted as (number of pets, number of siblings): $(0, 2)$, $(1, 1)$, $(2, 3)$ and $(3, 0)$. Which point is for a student who has more pets than siblings?
questions.solution: In each pair the first number is pets and the second is siblings. Only $(3, 0)$ has a first number larger than its second: 3 pets and 0 siblings. The others have fewer pets than siblings, or the same number.

solve.work: Pets > siblings: (0,2) no, (1,1) equal, (2,3) no, (3,0) yes.

questions.skill: Direction of an association
questions.stem: As the outside temperature rises, a café sells fewer hot drinks. A scatter plot of temperature (horizontal) and hot drinks sold (vertical) would show which kind of association?
choices: Positive: when one goes up, the other tends to go up
None: the two values are not related to each other at all
Negative: when one goes up, the other stays the same
Negative: when one goes up, the other tends to go down
questions.answer: Negative: when one goes up, the other tends to go down
questions.solution: Higher temperature goes with fewer hot drinks sold, so one value goes up while the other goes down. That is a negative association.

solve.answer: Negative: when one goes up, the other tends to go down
solve.work: Higher temperature goes with fewer hot drinks: negative, the other tends to go down.

questions.skill: Direction of an association
questions.stem: A candle is lit and measured each hour. The scatter plot of (hours burning, height in centimeters) has the points $(0, 20)$, $(1, 17)$, $(2, 13)$, $(3, 11)$ and $(4, 7)$. What is the direction of the association?
choices: Positive
No association
Negative
Perfectly horizontal
questions.answer: Negative
questions.solution: Reading the points from left to right, the heights fall: 20, 17, 13, 11, 7. When one value rises the other falls, so the association is negative.

solve.answer: Negative
solve.work: Heights 20, 17, 13, 11, 7 fall as hours rise: negative.

questions.skill: Direction of an association
questions.stem: A scatter plot of students' shoe sizes and their scores on a spelling test shows points spread all over the plot with no pattern. What does this suggest?
choices: Students with larger shoe sizes tend to score higher
Shoe size and spelling score have no association
Students with larger shoe sizes tend to score lower
Every student has the same score as their shoe size
questions.answer: Shoe size and spelling score have no association
questions.solution: Points scattered with no pattern mean that knowing one value does not help predict the other: there is no association.

solve.answer: Shoe size and spelling score have no association
solve.work: Points spread with no pattern means no association.

questions.skill: Direction of an association
questions.stem: Which pair of measurements would most likely show a positive association on a scatter plot?
choices: The number of pages read and the minutes spent reading
The speed of a car and the time it takes to drive 60 miles
A person's shoe size and the number of pets they own
The gas left in a tank and the miles driven since filling it
questions.answer: The number of pages read and the minutes spent reading
questions.solution: More pages usually take more minutes, so both values rise together: a positive association. A faster car takes less time (negative), shoe size and pets are unrelated, and gas left falls as miles are driven (negative).

solve.answer: The number of pages read and the minutes spent reading
solve.work: More minutes reading goes with more pages read: positive. Gas left vs miles is negative, shoe size vs pets none, speed vs time for 60 miles negative.

questions.skill: Form of an association
questions.stem: A taxi charges a start fee plus the same price for every mile. A scatter plot shows the total cost for 1, 2, 3 and 4 miles: 5, 7, 9 and 11 dollars. Which best describes the form of the pattern?
choices: Exponential: the cost is multiplied by the same factor each mile
Linear: the cost rises by the same amount each mile
Curved downward: the cost falls faster each mile
No pattern: the costs are scattered
questions.answer: Linear: the cost rises by the same amount each mile
questions.solution: The costs go up by 2 dollars every mile: $5, 7, 9, 11$. A constant change means a linear form.

solve.answer: Linear: the cost rises by the same amount each mile
solve.work: Costs 5, 7, 9, 11 rise by 2 each mile: linear.

questions.skill: Form of an association
questions.stem: A scientist counts bacteria in a dish at hours 0, 1, 2 and 3 and finds 5, 10, 20 and 40. The count doubles every hour. What form will a scatter plot of the counts against the hours have?
choices: Linear: the counts rise by the same amount every single hour
Exponential decay: the counts fall by a smaller amount each hour
No pattern: the counts are scattered with no clear trend
Exponential growth: the counts rise faster and faster
questions.answer: Exponential growth: the counts rise faster and faster
questions.solution: Each count is 2 times the one before, so the increases get bigger each hour (5, 10, 20). A constant factor means exponential growth.

solve.answer: Exponential growth: the counts rise faster and faster
solve.work: 5, 10, 20, 40 doubles each hour: exponential growth, rising faster and faster.

questions.skill: Strength of an association
questions.stem: In scatter plot A the points lie very close to a straight line that rises. In scatter plot B the points are spread widely but still rise a little. Which statement is true?
choices: Plot A shows the stronger association
Plot B shows the stronger association
Both plots show equally strong associations because both rise
Neither plot shows an association because the points are not exactly on a line
questions.answer: Plot A shows the stronger association
questions.solution: The closer the points are to a line or curve, the stronger the association. Plot A's points hug a line, so plot A is stronger.

solve.answer: Plot A shows the stronger association
solve.work: Strength is how closely points follow a pattern; A's points lie very close to the line, so A is stronger.

questions.skill: Strength of an association
questions.stem: Which description matches a strong association between two variables?
choices: The points follow a line that is very steep, going up fast
The points are spread out across the whole plot, edge to edge
The points stay close to a line or a smooth curve
The plot contains a very large number of points
questions.answer: The points stay close to a line or a smooth curve
questions.solution: Strength is about how closely the points follow a pattern. Steepness and the number of points do not measure strength, and widely spread points mean a weak association.

solve.answer: The points stay close to a line or a smooth curve
solve.work: A strong association means points stay close to a line or smooth curve; steepness and number of points do not matter.

questions.skill: Judging an informal line of best fit
questions.stem: Which describes a good informal line of best fit for a scatter plot with a linear pattern?
choices: It passes through the first and last points, whatever the other points do
It keeps every point above it, so that no point is hidden behind the line
It always passes through the origin, where both axes are equal to 0
It follows the trend of the points, with about as many points above it as below it
questions.answer: It follows the trend of the points, with about as many points above it as below it
questions.solution: A line of best fit should follow the overall trend, staying close to the points with roughly equal numbers above and below. It need not pass through any particular point or the origin.

solve.answer: It follows the trend of the points, with about as many points above it as below it
solve.work: A good informal fit follows the trend with roughly equal numbers of points above and below.

questions.skill: Judging an informal line of best fit
questions.stem: The points $(2, 4)$, $(4, 8)$, $(6, 12)$ and $(8, 16)$ all lie on the line $y = mx$. What is the value of $m$?
questions.solution: Substitute a point: $4 = m \times 2$, so $m = 4 \div 2 = 2$. The other points agree: $8 \div 4 = 2$, $12 \div 6 = 2$ and $16 \div 8 = 2$.

questions.skill: Predicting from a line of best fit
