questions.stem: With all 12 points, the slope of the least-squares line is 0.8. With one outlier removed, it is 2.3. By how much did the slope change when the outlier was removed?
questions.solution: 2.3 - 0.8 = 1.5, so that one point changed the slope a lot.

questions.skill: Outliers and influential points
questions.stem: A student wants to delete a point because it lowers the correlation. When is it reasonable to remove it?
choices: Whenever it lowers $r$, as the goal is to get the highest $r$ possible
Never, because points can never be removed
Whenever it lies on the left side of the plot
Only with a good reason, such as a known recording error
questions.answer: Only with a good reason, such as a known recording error
questions.solution: A point should be removed only if there is a reason to believe it is an error or does not belong. Otherwise it should be kept, perhaps reporting the results both ways.

solve.answer: Only with a good reason, such as a known recording error
solve.work: Remove only with a good reason, e.g. recording error.

questions.skill: Correlation versus causation
questions.stem: Sales of heaters and sales of wool hats both rise in December. What is the best explanation?
choices: Buying heaters makes people go out and buy wool hats too
Buying wool hats makes people buy heaters
The two are not linked in any way
A third variable, cold weather, influences both
questions.answer: A third variable, cold weather, influences both
questions.solution: Cold weather affects both. This is a lurking variable rather than one product causing the other.

solve.answer: A third variable, cold weather, influences both
solve.work: Cold weather is a lurking variable for both.

questions.skill: Correlation versus causation
questions.stem: An observational study finds a strong positive correlation between time spent on a learning app and test scores. Which statement is supported?
choices: Students who spend more time on the app tend to have higher scores
Spending more time on the app will raise the score of any single student
Higher test scores make students want to spend much more time on the app
App time is the only thing that affects test scores
questions.answer: Students who spend more time on the app tend to have higher scores
questions.solution: Observational data support a statement about association only, not about cause.

solve.answer: Students who spend more time on the app tend to have higher scores

questions.skill: Correlation versus causation
questions.stem: In an observational study of 500 students, 300 used a reading app and 200 did not. Of the users, 240 passed the test. Of the non-users, 120 passed. By how many percentage points is the users' pass rate higher than the non-users' pass rate?
questions.solution: Users: 240 / 300 = 80 percent. Non-users: 120 / 200 = 60 percent. The difference is 20 percentage points. Because students chose whether to use the app, this shows an association but does not prove the app caused it.

questions.skill: Correlation versus causation
questions.stem: A study only observed teens and did not assign them to any group. Which headline claims more than the study can show?
choices: Teens who eat breakfast tend to do better in school
Eating breakfast makes teens do better in school
Breakfast and school grades are linked in a survey of teens
Teens who skip breakfast are less likely to have top grades
questions.answer: Eating breakfast makes teens do better in school
questions.solution: "Makes" claims a cause. The other headlines describe only an association.

solve.answer: Eating breakfast makes teens do better in school

questions.skill: Making and judging predictions
questions.stem: A line is fit to a park's number of visitors each month from March to October. A planner uses it to predict visitors in December. Which statement is best?
choices: It is reliable because the line is a least-squares line
It is reliable because December comes right after October
It is unreliable only when the correlation is negative
It is risky, since December is outside the months studied
questions.answer: It is risky, since December is outside the months studied
questions.solution: December is outside the range of the data, and visitor patterns in winter may be very different from the months studied.

solve.answer: It is risky, since December is outside the months studied
solve.work: December is outside March-October: extrapolation, risky.

questions.skill: Making and judging predictions
questions.stem: The line $\hat{y} = 2.4x + 18$ is fit to data. For what value of $x$ does the line predict $y = 66$?

questions.skill: Making and judging predictions
questions.stem: Which prediction is the most trustworthy?
choices: A prediction from a line with $r = 0.95$ at an $x$-value inside the data's range
A prediction from a line with $r = 0.3$ at an $x$-value inside the data's range
A prediction from a line with $r = 0.95$ at an $x$-value far outside the data's range
A prediction from a line with $r = 0.3$ at an $x$-value far outside the data's range
questions.answer: A prediction from a line with $r = 0.95$ at an $x$-value inside the data's range
questions.solution: Reliable predictions need a strong relationship and an $x$-value within the range of the data.

solve.answer: A prediction from a line with $r = 0.95$ at an $x$-value inside the data's range

questions.skill: Outliers and influential points
questions.stem: The least-squares line $\hat{y} = 4x + 10$ is used for three students. At $x = 2$ the actual $y$ is 19, at $x = 5$ it is 31, and at $x = 8$ it is 70. One of the three points is an outlier. What is that point's residual (actual value minus predicted value)?
questions.solution: The line predicts 18, 30 and 42. The residuals are $19 - 18 = 1$, $31 - 30 = 1$ and $70 - 42 = 28$. The point at $x = 8$ is far from the line, so it is the outlier, and its residual is 28.

solve.work: Predictions: x=2 -> 18, x=5 -> 30, x=8 -> 42. Residuals: 19-18=1, 31-30=1, 70-42=28. The outlier is (8,70), residual 28.

questions.skill: Outliers and influential points
questions.stem: A least-squares line fit to all of a data set is $\hat{y} = 1.2x + 9$. After one outlier is removed, the new line is $\hat{y} = 2x + 5$. At $x = 10$, how much greater is the prediction from the new line than the prediction from the line fit to all of the data?
questions.solution: The line fit to all of the data predicts $1.2(10) + 9 = 21$. The new line predicts $2(10) + 5 = 25$. The difference is $25 - 21 = 4$, so the outlier pulled the prediction down by 4.

solve.work: New line at x=10: 2(10)+5=25. Old line: 1.2(10)+9=21. Difference 25-21=4.

questions.skill: Effect of an outlier on correlation
questions.stem: For a set of 20 data points, $r = 0.45$. After one point that lies far from the pattern is removed, $r$ becomes $0.92$. What does this suggest about that point?
choices: It proved that the two variables are not related
Removing any point always raises the correlation
It was an outlier that was weakening the linear pattern
The two variables now cause each other
questions.answer: It was an outlier that was weakening the linear pattern
questions.solution: The remaining 19 points follow a strong linear pattern ($r = 0.92$). The one point far from it pulled the correlation down, so it is an outlier. Removing a point does not always raise $r$, and a correlation never proves cause.

solve.answer: It was an outlier that was weakening the linear pattern
solve.work: Removing one far-off point raised r from 0.45 to 0.92, so that point was an outlier weakening the linear pattern.

questions.skill: Evaluating an exponential model
questions.stem: The value of a car is modeled by $V = 20{,}000(0.9)^t$, where $V$ is its value in dollars and $t$ is its age in years. What is the value of the car after 2 years, in dollars?

questions.skill: Reading a residual plot
questions.stem: A residual plot for a linear model shows the residuals forming a clear U-shaped curve instead of a random scatter around 0. What does this suggest?
choices: A straight line is not the best model; a curve may fit better
The linear model fits the data perfectly
The correlation coefficient must be exactly 0
Every data point is an outlier
questions.answer: A straight line is not the best model; a curve may fit better
questions.solution: A good linear model leaves residuals scattered randomly around 0. A clear curved pattern in the residuals means the data bend away from a straight line, so a curved model, such as an exponential one, may fit better.

solve.answer: A straight line is not the best model; a curve may fit better
solve.work: A curved pattern in residuals means the linear model misses curvature; a nonlinear model may fit better.

questions.skill: Least-squares line: meaning and prediction
questions.stem: A data set has a mean $x$-value of 20 and a mean $y$-value of 65. Its least-squares line has slope 1.5. What $y$-value does the line predict when $x = 30$?
questions.solution: The line passes through (20, 65). Going from $x = 20$ to $x = 30$ is 10 units, which adds $1.5 \times 10 = 15$. So $y = 65 + 15 = 80$.

questions.skill: Least-squares line: meaning and prediction
questions.stem: A least-squares line $\hat{y} = 8x + 120$ predicts a seedling's height $\hat{y}$ in millimeters after $x$ days. How tall, in centimeters, does the line predict the seedling to be after 15 days?
questions.solution: $8(15) + 120 = 240$ millimeters. There are 10 millimeters in a centimeter, so 240 / 10 = 24 centimeters.

questions.skill: Least-squares line: meaning and prediction
questions.stem: A calculator reports a regression equation of the form $y = a + bx$ with $a = 42.5$ and $b = -0.8$. What value of $y$ does the equation predict for $x = 25$?

questions.skill: Least-squares line: meaning and prediction
questions.stem: Which statement is true of every least-squares line?
choices: It passes through the first data point in the list of data
It always has a slope that is equal to the correlation $r$
It passes through the point (mean of $x$, mean of $y$)
It always passes through the origin of the plot, $(0, 0)$
questions.answer: It passes through the point (mean of $x$, mean of $y$)
questions.solution: A least-squares line always goes through (mean of $x$, mean of $y$). The slope equals $r$ only in special cases, and the line need not pass through any data point or the origin.

solve.answer: It passes through the point (mean of $x$, mean of $y$)

questions.skill: Exponential models
questions.stem: A patch of algae covers 3 square meters and triples in area every day, so its area after $t$ days is $3(3)^t$ square meters. After how many days will it cover 243 square meters?

questions.skill: Exponential models
questions.stem: A town has 4000 people and grows 25 percent per year, so $P = 4000(1.25)^t$. How many more people does the town have after 2 years than it has now?

questions.skill: Exponential models
questions.stem: For $x = 0, 1, 2, 3$ the values of $y$ are 80, 48, 28.8, 17.28. Which equation fits these data?
questions.solution: Each value is 0.6 times the one before (48/80 = 0.6, 28.8/48 = 0.6, 17.28/28.8 = 0.6). The 0.4 would be the rate of decrease, not the factor.

questions.skill: Exponential models
questions.stem: Money in a fund doubles every 3 years, so $A = 800(2)^{t/3}$, where $t$ is the number of years. How many dollars are in the fund after 6 years?
questions.solution: For $t = 6$ the exponent is $6/3 = 2$, so $A = 800 \times 2^2 = 800 \times 4 = 3200$ dollars.

questions.skill: Correlation coefficient: sign and strength
questions.stem: A student swaps the two variables, using the old $y$-values as $x$ and the old $x$-values as $y$. What happens to $r$?
choices: It changes sign
It becomes its reciprocal
It stays the same
It drops to 0
questions.answer: It stays the same
questions.solution: The correlation between $x$ and $y$ is the same as the correlation between $y$ and $x$.

solve.answer: It stays the same
solve.work: r is symmetric in x and y: stays the same.

questions.skill: Correlation coefficient: sign and strength
questions.stem: A data set has $r = 0.8$. Every $x$-value is replaced by its opposite (each $x$ becomes $-x$). What is the new value of $r$?
questions.solution: Replacing $x$ by $-x$ turns a rising pattern into a falling one with the same tightness. So $r$ becomes $-0.8$.

questions.skill: Correlation coefficient: sign and strength
questions.stem: For a large data set, $r = 0.97$. Which conclusion is justified?
choices: Changes in $x$ are the cause of all of the changes in $y$
97 percent of the points lie on the line
$y$ increases by 0.97 for every 1-unit increase in $x$
There is a very strong positive linear association
questions.answer: There is a very strong positive linear association
questions.solution: An $r$ near 1 describes a strong positive linear association only. It does not prove cause, give the percent of points on the line, or give the slope.

solve.answer: There is a very strong positive linear association
solve.work: r=0.97 means very strong positive linear association; not slope, not causation, not percent on line.

questions.skill: Correlation coefficient: sign and strength
questions.stem: For a sample of students, the correlation between hours of TV per week and test score is $r = -0.78$. Which interpretation is correct?
choices: Students with more TV time tend to have clearly lower scores
Each hour of TV watched lowers a student's score by 0.78 points
Seventy-eight percent of the students watch a lot of TV each week
TV is only a weak influence on scores because $r$ is negative
questions.answer: Students with more TV time tend to have clearly lower scores
questions.solution: A negative $r$ with $|r|$ fairly close to 1 shows a fairly strong negative association. $r$ is not a slope or a percent of students.

solve.answer: Students with more TV time tend to have clearly lower scores
solve.work: Negative, fairly strong: more TV tends to go with lower scores.

questions.skill: Residuals and residual plots
questions.stem: A residual plot shows points close to zero for small values of $x$, but spreading farther and farther from zero as $x$ increases. What does this indicate?
choices: Predictions are much less precise for large values of $x$
The model is nearly perfect for the large values of $x$ in the data
The data set must contain no outliers at all, even for large $x$
The relationship between the two variables is negative overall
questions.answer: Predictions are much less precise for large values of $x$
questions.solution: Residuals that grow in size as $x$ grows mean the errors in prediction are bigger for large $x$.

solve.answer: Predictions are much less precise for large values of $x$
solve.work: Fan shape: spread grows with x, so predictions less precise for large x.

questions.skill: Residuals and residual plots
questions.stem: A least-squares line is fit to four data points. Three of the residuals are 3, $-5$ and 4. What is the fourth residual?
questions.solution: The residuals from a least-squares line always add to 0. So 3 + (-5) + 4 + r = 0, which gives 2 + r = 0 and r = -2.

solve.issues: Relies on residuals of a least-squares line summing to 0, a fact not always taught in Math 1; fine if taught.
solve.work: LSRL residuals sum to 0: 3-5+4=2, so fourth=-2.

questions.skill: Residuals and residual plots
questions.stem: The line $\hat{y} = 0.8x + 12$ is used to predict a score. A student with $x = 35$ actually scores 38. By how many points does the line overestimate this student's score?
questions.solution: Predicted: 0.8(35) + 12 = 28 + 12 = 40. The actual score is 38, so the line overestimates by 40 - 38 = 2 points.

questions.skill: Residuals and residual plots
questions.stem: The scatter plot of bacteria counts rises in a curve that gets steeper. The residual plot for a linear model shows positive, then negative, then positive residuals in a clear curved pattern. Which model should be tried next?
choices: A linear model with a smaller intercept
An exponential model, because the counts keep rising faster
A linear model with a negative slope
The same linear model with more decimal places
questions.answer: An exponential model, because the counts keep rising faster
questions.solution: A curved pattern in the residuals means the line is the wrong kind of model. Counts that rise ever faster suggest an exponential model.

solve.answer: An exponential model, because the counts keep rising faster
solve.work: Curved residual pattern, accelerating growth: exponential.

questions.skill: Residuals and residual plots
questions.stem: For the same data, Model A has residuals 1, $-2$, 2, $-1$ and Model B has residuals 4, $-3$, 5, $-6$. Which statement is true?
choices: Both fit equally well because both sets of residuals add to 0
Model B fits better because its residuals are larger
Model A fits better because its residuals are closer to 0
Model A fits worse because its residuals are mostly small
questions.answer: Model A fits better because its residuals are closer to 0
questions.solution: Both sets add to 0, but that does not show a good fit. Model A's residuals are much smaller in size, so it fits the data more closely.

solve.answer: Model A fits better because its residuals are closer to 0
solve.work: A residuals smaller in size (sum of squares 10 vs 86): A fits better.

questions.skill: Outliers and influential points
questions.stem: Which kind of point is the most likely to change the slope of the least-squares line a lot?
choices: A point with an $x$-value far from the others and well off the pattern
A point in the middle of the range of $x$-values and right on the pattern
A point near the mean of $x$ whose residual from the line is also very small
Any point with a positive residual of about 1
questions.answer: A point with an $x$-value far from the others and well off the pattern
questions.solution: A point far out in the $x$-direction acts like a long lever, so if it is off the pattern it can tilt the line.

solve.answer: A point with an $x$-value far from the others and well off the pattern
solve.work: High leverage and off pattern: most influential.

questions.skill: Outliers and influential points
questions.stem: Removing point A changes the slope of a line from 2.0 to 1.9. Removing point B changes the slope from 2.0 to 0.4. Which statement is best?
choices: Point A is much more influential on the line than point B is
Point B is much more influential on the line than point A
Both points are equally influential on the line as a whole
Neither of the two points has any influence on the line at all
questions.answer: Point B is much more influential on the line than point A
questions.solution: The slope hardly changes without A but changes a great deal without B, so B has the greater influence.

solve.answer: Point B is much more influential on the line than point A
solve.work: B changes slope by 1.6 vs 0.1: B much more influential.

questions.skill: Outliers and influential points
questions.stem: A point is far to the right of the other points, yet it lies right on the line that fits the others. How does removing it affect the least-squares line?
choices: A lot, because it is so far away from the mean of $x$
The slope of the line would reverse its sign entirely
Hardly at all, since it follows the pattern of the others
The line would then have to pass through the origin
questions.answer: Hardly at all, since it follows the pattern of the others
questions.solution: A point that is far out but follows the pattern of the others supports the same line, so removing it changes the line very little.

solve.answer: Hardly at all, since it follows the pattern of the others
solve.work: On the line through the others: removing it hardly changes the line.

questions.skill: Correlation versus causation
questions.stem: A study of 1,000 adults finds that those who take daily vitamins have fewer colds. What is the strongest reason this study cannot show that vitamins prevent colds?
choices: One thousand adults are far too many people to compare
Colds are impossible to count in a group of adults
People who take vitamins may also exercise and sleep more
Vitamins cannot be treated as a variable in any study
questions.answer: People who take vitamins may also exercise and sleep more
questions.solution: People chose whether to take vitamins, so other habits that affect health may differ between the groups.

solve.answer: People who take vitamins may also exercise and sleep more

questions.skill: Correlation versus causation
questions.stem: To decide whether a tutoring program causes better grades, which study design is the most convincing?
choices: Compare the grades of students who signed up with those who did not
Ask all of the tutored students whether they felt that it helped
Compare this year's tutored students with last year's untutored students overall
Randomly assign volunteers to tutoring or none, then compare grade changes
questions.answer: Randomly assign volunteers to tutoring or none, then compare grade changes
questions.solution: Random assignment is what allows a difference in outcomes to be credited to the program.

solve.answer: Randomly assign volunteers to tutoring or none, then compare grade changes

questions.skill: Correlation versus causation
questions.stem: In a randomized experiment, 80 plants are split at random into two equal groups. The plants given fertilizer average 24 centimeters tall and the others average 20 centimeters. Because the groups were formed at random, the difference can be credited to the fertilizer. How many centimeters taller, on average, are the fertilized plants?
questions.solution: 24 - 20 = 4 centimeters.

solve.issues: Trivial subtraction; the causal reasoning is given in the stem.

questions.skill: Correlation versus causation
questions.stem: Over 20 years, the number of cell phone owners in a town and the number of pizza shops both grew steadily, and their correlation is $r = 0.98$. What is the best conclusion?
choices: Both grew over time, so the correlation does not show cause
Pizza shops cause more people to want to buy their own cell phones
Cell phones cause new pizza shops to open in the town each year
The correlation must be wrong because it is above 0.9
questions.answer: Both grew over time, so the correlation does not show cause
questions.solution: Two quantities that both grow with time can be strongly correlated without either causing the other.

solve.answer: Both grew over time, so the correlation does not show cause

questions.skill: Making and judging predictions
questions.stem: A model predicts a sale price of 250 thousand dollars, but the house actually sells for 200 thousand dollars. By what percent of the actual price did the model overestimate?
questions.solution: The overestimate is 250 - 200 = 50. As a percent of the actual price: 50 / 200 = 0.25, which is 25 percent.

questions.skill: Making and judging predictions
questions.stem: A phone's value is modeled by $V = 800(0.75)^t$ dollars after $t$ years. How many dollars of value does the model say the phone loses in its first 2 years?
questions.solution: $(0.75)^2 = 0.5625$, so $V = 800 \times 0.5625 = 450$ after 2 years. The loss is 800 - 450 = 350 dollars.

questions.skill: Making and judging predictions
questions.stem: A virus count was 100, 200, 400 and 800 on days 0, 1, 2 and 3. Both a linear model and an exponential model are fitted. Which will predict day 6 better?
choices: The linear model, because it takes much less work to calculate
The exponential model, because the count doubles each day
Both equally, because four points can fit either kind of model
Neither, because four data points are not enough to build a model
questions.answer: The exponential model, because the count doubles each day
questions.solution: The count doubles every day, so the pattern is exponential. The exponential model predicts 100 x 2^6 = 6,400, while a line would predict far less.

solve.answer: The exponential model, because the count doubles each day

questions.skill: Making and judging predictions
questions.stem: A linear model has residuals within $\pm 2$ for $x$ between 0 and 20. At $x = 30$ the actual value is 15 higher than the model predicts. What should you conclude?
choices: The line is still reliable since it is a least-squares line
The data point at $x = 30$ must have been recorded wrongly
The line is unreliable for larger $x$ values like 30, so another model may be needed
The line is reliable as long as its slope is positive
questions.answer: The line is unreliable for larger $x$ values like 30, so another model may be needed
questions.solution: The model worked well within the range 0 to 20 but fails badly at 30, so using it for larger $x$ is unreliable.

solve.answer: The line is unreliable for larger $x$ values like 30, so another model may be needed
solve.work: Large residual outside the fitted range: line unreliable there.

questions.skill: Outliers and influential points
questions.stem: An analyst flags a point as an outlier when its actual $y$ is more than 12 units away from the value the line predicts. The least-squares line is $\hat{y} = 2.5x + 8$. A new point has $x = 10$. What is the least whole-number $y$ that would make this point an outlier above the line?
questions.solution: At $x = 10$ the line predicts $2.5(10) + 8 = 33$. A point is an outlier above the line when $y$ is more than $33 + 12 = 45$. The least whole number greater than 45 is 46.

solve.work: Predicted y = 2.5(10)+8 = 33. Outlier above the line needs y - 33 > 12, so y > 45. Least whole number is 46.

questions.skill: Making and judging predictions
questions.stem: A population is modeled by $P = 400(1.5)^t$, where $t$ is the number of years after the start, so $t = 0$ at the start. What is the least whole number $t$ for which the model gives $P > 2000$?
questions.solution: Try whole numbers. $t = 3$ gives $400 \times 3.375 = 1350$, which is not above 2000. $t = 4$ gives $400 \times 5.0625 = 2025$, which is above 2000. So the least whole number is 4.

questions.skill: Reporting a conclusion accurately
questions.stem: In a random sample of 100 students, 60 said they prefer online homework. Which statement reports this accurately?
choices: 60 percent of all students everywhere prefer online homework
Online homework is better for learning
Exactly 60 percent of the students in the school prefer online homework
In the sample, 60 percent of the students prefer online homework
questions.answer: In the sample, 60 percent of the students prefer online homework
questions.solution: The data tell us what happened in the sample: 60 of 100 students prefer online homework. They do not show that online homework is better for learning, and a sample cannot tell us the exact percent for everyone.

solve.answer: In the sample, 60 percent of the students prefer online homework
solve.work: 60/100 = 60 percent of the sample. The other options over-generalize, claim exactness for the school, or claim causation.

questions.skill: Steps of a statistical investigation
questions.stem: A class carries out a statistical investigation. Which step should come first?
choices: Collect the data
Pose a statistical question
Analyze the data
Share the conclusions
questions.answer: Pose a statistical question
questions.solution: An investigation starts by asking a question that data can answer. Then the data are collected, analyzed, and the conclusions are shared.

solve.answer: Pose a statistical question
solve.work: The investigation process begins with posing a statistical question, then collecting, analyzing, interpreting/sharing.

questions.skill: Steps of a statistical investigation
questions.stem: The steps of a statistical investigation are numbered. 1: ask a question that data can answer. 2: plan the study and collect data. 3: analyze the data. 4: communicate the conclusions. Ana makes a bar graph of her data and finds its median. Which step number is she working on?
questions.solution: Making graphs and finding summary numbers such as the median is analysis of data that were already collected. That is step 3.

solve.work: Making a bar graph and finding a median are analysis of the data, which is step 3.

questions.skill: Steps of a statistical investigation
questions.stem: Mia has finished collecting data on how long students take to get to school. Which step of her investigation comes next?
choices: Analyzing the data with graphs and summary numbers
Writing the question that her investigation will try to answer
Deciding which students to include in her survey group
Presenting her conclusions before she looks at the data
questions.answer: Analyzing the data with graphs and summary numbers
questions.solution: The steps go in order: ask a question, plan and collect data, analyze, then communicate. Collecting is done, so analyzing comes next. Conclusions cannot be presented before the data are analyzed.

solve.answer: Analyzing the data with graphs and summary numbers
solve.work: After collecting data, the next step is analyzing it (graphs, summary numbers). The other options are earlier steps or out of order.

questions.skill: Steps of a statistical investigation
questions.stem: Which action belongs to the step of communicating the results of an investigation?
choices: Deciding how many students to include in the survey group
Writing the question that the survey will ask each student
Entering each student's answers into a spreadsheet
Explaining what the data show and what they cannot show
questions.answer: Explaining what the data show and what they cannot show
questions.solution: Communicating means telling others what was found, including how far the results can be trusted. Choosing a sample, writing the survey question and entering answers all happen earlier in the investigation.

solve.answer: Explaining what the data show and what they cannot show
solve.work: Communicating = explaining conclusions and their limits. Writing questions and choosing the sample are planning; entering answers is data handling.

questions.skill: Evaluating how data were collected
questions.stem: Which survey question is worded most fairly?
choices: Don't you agree that walking to school is the healthiest choice?
Wouldn't you say that riding the slow, crowded bus is awful?
Why is biking to school so much better than riding in a car?
How do you usually get to school: walk, bike, bus, or car?
questions.answer: How do you usually get to school: walk, bike, bus, or car?
questions.solution: A fair question does not push people toward one answer. The question that simply lists the ways to get to school is neutral. The others suggest which answer is right.

solve.answer: How do you usually get to school: walk, bike, bus, or car?
solve.work: The other three are leading or loaded questions. The neutral one lists choices without judgment.

questions.skill: Evaluating how data were collected
questions.stem: A class gave out 80 surveys and 60 of them were returned. What percent of the surveys were returned?
questions.solution: Divide the number returned by the number given out: $60 \div 80 = 0.75$, which is 75 percent.

questions.skill: Reporting results accurately
questions.stem: Which sentence gives a result that readers can understand without anything else?
choices: The median was 25 for the students who were asked about their reading.
The 30 students surveyed read for a median of 25 minutes per night.
Students read for a very long time each night, as the survey showed.
The reading time for every student in the whole school was 25 minutes.
questions.answer: The 30 students surveyed read for a median of 25 minutes per night.
questions.solution: A clear report says who was measured, what was measured, and the unit. Only one sentence names the 30 students, the median, and minutes per night. The others leave out the unit, are vague, or claim more than a sample can show.

solve.answer: The 30 students surveyed read for a median of 25 minutes per night.
solve.work: Option 1 names the sample (30 students surveyed), the statistic (median), value and units (25 minutes per night). Others lack units, are vague, or overgeneralize.

questions.skill: Reporting results accurately
questions.stem: A survey asked 40 students to name a favorite subject. Math was chosen by 18, science by 12 and art by 10. Consider three statements. (1) Math was chosen by more students than any other subject. (2) Fewer than half of the students chose math. (3) Art was chosen by 10 percent of the students. How many of the three statements are correct?
questions.solution: Statement 1 is correct because 18 is greater than 12 and 10. Statement 2 is correct because half of 40 is 20 and 18 is less than 20. Statement 3 is not correct because $10 \div 40 = 25$ percent. Two statements are correct.

solve.work: (1) 18 > 12 and 18 > 10: true. (2) Half of 40 is 20; 18 < 20: true. (3) 10/40 = 25%, not 10%: false. Two correct.

questions.skill: Limits of conclusions
questions.stem: A survey asked every one of the 30 students in Ms. Lee's class about their favorite game. To which group can its results be applied with the most confidence?
choices: All of the students in Ms. Lee's school
The 30 students in Ms. Lee's class
All of the students in Ms. Lee's state
All of the students in the whole country
questions.answer: The 30 students in Ms. Lee's class
questions.solution: Everyone in the class was asked, so the results describe that class. Applying them to a whole school, a state or a country would go beyond the group that was surveyed.

solve.answer: The 30 students in Ms. Lee's class
solve.work: Every student in the class was surveyed (a census of the class), so the results describe exactly those 30 students; generalizing further is unsupported.

questions.skill: Limits of conclusions
questions.stem: Tom asks 5 of his friends if they like soccer, and all 5 say yes. He writes, "Everyone in our school likes soccer." What is wrong with his conclusion?
choices: He should have asked fewer friends so that the answers were more exact.
He should have written that no one in the school likes soccer.
He asked only five friends, who cannot speak for the whole school.
Nothing is wrong, since all five of the people he asked agreed.
questions.answer: He asked only five friends, who cannot speak for the whole school.
questions.solution: Five friends are a very small group, and friends often share interests. They cannot show what the whole school thinks.

solve.answer: He asked only five friends, who cannot speak for the whole school.
solve.work: Five friends is a small, non-random sample; cannot generalize to the whole school.

questions.skill: Limits of conclusions
questions.stem: A survey finds that households with more books tend to have children who read better. Consider three statements. (1) In this group, children from households with more books tended to read better. (2) Buying more books for a home will make a child read better. (3) Children who read better cause their parents to buy more books. How many of the three statements does the survey support?
questions.solution: The survey only shows a pattern in the group studied, so statement 1 is supported. It cannot show that buying books causes better reading (statement 2) or that reading causes book buying (statement 3). One statement is supported.

solve.work: A survey shows association only. (1) restates the association: supported. (2) and (3) are causal claims in either direction: not supported. Count = 1.

questions.skill: Choosing a summary or display
questions.stem: A class wants to show how many students chose each of four pizza toppings. Which display is best?
choices: A line graph that connects the four toppings
A scatter plot with one dot for each student
A bar graph with one bar for each topping
A box plot of the number of students per topping
questions.answer: A bar graph with one bar for each topping
questions.solution: Toppings are categories, and a bar graph gives each category its own bar so the counts can be compared. A line graph suggests change over time, and a scatter plot shows pairs of numbers.

solve.answer: A bar graph with one bar for each topping
solve.work: Counts of a categorical variable: bar graph, one bar per topping.

questions.skill: Choosing a summary or display
questions.stem: Which display is best for showing how the temperature in a town changed hour by hour during one day?
choices: A pie chart with one slice for each hour
A line graph with the hour on the horizontal axis
A bar graph that shows only the day's single highest temperature
A list of the day's highest and lowest temperatures only
questions.answer: A line graph with the hour on the horizontal axis
questions.solution: A line graph shows change over time, so it shows how temperatures rose and fell hour by hour. A pie chart shows parts of a whole, and the other choices leave out the hourly changes.

solve.answer: A line graph with the hour on the horizontal axis
solve.work: Change over time: line graph with time on the horizontal axis.

questions.skill: Critiquing a percent claim in the media
questions.stem: A report says that cases of a rare allergy rose 300%. Which information would best help you judge how serious the rise is?
choices: The actual number of cases before and after the rise
The number of people who read the report and the date it was printed
The names of the doctors who saw the allergy cases in the town
The percent of readers who like the news site that printed the story
questions.answer: The actual number of cases before and after the rise
questions.solution: A large percent can come from a small start. If cases rose from 1 to 4, that is a 300 percent rise but only 3 more cases. The actual counts show how serious it is.

solve.answer: The actual number of cases before and after the rise
solve.work: A large percent rise on a tiny base may be few cases; the actual counts are needed.

questions.skill: Applying a sample result to a population
questions.stem: In a sample of 50 students, 10 walk to school. The school has 500 students. If the sample is typical, about how many students at the school walk to school?
questions.solution: In the sample, $10 \div 50 = 0.2$, or 20 percent walk. Then $0.2 \times 500 = 100$ students at the school.

questions.skill: Applying a sample result to a population
questions.stem: A survey of a random sample finds that 30 percent of students like the new schedule. If the school has 1,200 students, about how many students like it?
questions.solution: Take 30 percent of the whole school: $0.3 \times 1200 = 360$ students.

questions.skill: Evaluating how data were collected
questions.stem: Kai asked 5 students for their favorite sport. Lena asked 60 students who were chosen at random from the school. Whose result is likely to describe the whole school better, and why?
choices: Lena's, because a larger random sample is more likely to match the whole school
Kai's, because a small group of students gives answers that are more exact than a large group's
Kai's, because five answers are easier to check than sixty
Neither, because a sample can never describe a whole school
questions.answer: Lena's, because a larger random sample is more likely to match the whole school
questions.solution: A larger sample chosen at random usually gives a better estimate for the whole school than five students. A sample can describe a larger group when it is chosen well.

solve.answer: Lena's, because a larger random sample is more likely to match the whole school
solve.work: Lena's sample is random and larger, so it is more likely to represent the school. Neither claim 'never describe' nor small-is-exact is right.

questions.skill: Limits of conclusions
questions.stem: Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise during the summer months. Does this show that eating ice cream causes sunburn?
choices: No; both may rise because of a third thing, hot and sunny weather.
Yes; things that rise together at the same time of year are always caused by one another.
Yes; people get sunburned right after they eat ice cream outdoors, so the ice cream is the cause.
No; two things that rise together can never be related in any way, because patterns are only chance.
questions.answer: No; both may rise because of a third thing, hot and sunny weather.
questions.solution: Two things can rise together because a third thing affects both. Hot, sunny weather leads to more ice cream sales and more sunburns. A pattern alone does not show that one thing causes the other.

solve.answer: No; both may rise because of a third thing, hot and sunny weather.
solve.work: Correlation, not causation; lurking variable is hot sunny weather driving both.

questions.skill: Critiquing a percent claim in the media
questions.stem: A poster says, "Our class improved 200 percent!" Which question should you ask first to judge the claim?
choices: What day of the week was the poster put up in the hallway, and who made it?
What is the favorite subject of the students in the class, and of their teacher?
How many days long is the school year at the school that made the poster?
What was the starting score, and how many students are in the class that made the poster?
questions.answer: What was the starting score, and how many students are in the class that made the poster?
questions.solution: A percent change depends on the starting amount. A rise from 1 point to 3 points is 200 percent, but it is still a tiny score. The starting score and the size of the class show how much the claim means.

solve.answer: What was the starting score, and how many students are in the class that made the poster?
solve.issues: Minor: the second half (class size) is less relevant than the starting score, but the option is still clearly the best.
solve.work: A percent increase depends on the base: 200% of a tiny starting score could be small. Need the starting score. Only option addressing this.

questions.skill: Critiquing an average in the media
questions.stem: A report says that the average commute in a city is 20 minutes. Which extra information would help you most to judge how long YOUR commute might take?
choices: How many cars are registered to the people who live in the city, and of what kind
How spread out the commute times are, such as the shortest and the longest
What the average commute is in a city in another country, such as a very large one
What time of day the news report about the commutes was written and who wrote it
questions.answer: How spread out the commute times are, such as the shortest and the longest
questions.solution: An average alone hides how much the values vary. Knowing the shortest and longest commutes shows whether most people are near 20 minutes or far from it.

solve.answer: How spread out the commute times are, such as the shortest and the longest
solve.work: Knowing the spread (min, max, variability) tells how far an individual commute may be from 20 minutes.

questions.skill: Critiquing an average in the media
questions.stem: A store ad says, "Our customers are the happiest: average rating 4.8 out of 5." The ratings are 5 reviews, all written by friends of the store owner. What is the main problem with the claim?
choices: An average rating cannot be found when the highest rating on the scale is as large as 5
The average should have been given as a whole number only, because ratings are whole numbers
The ratings come from only five people, all friends of the owner, who are not a fair sample of the customers
The ad should have used the lowest rating instead of the average, because it is more honest
questions.answer: The ratings come from only five people, all friends of the owner, who are not a fair sample of the customers
questions.solution: An average is only as good as the data behind it. Five reviews from the owner's friends do not represent the store's customers.

solve.answer: The ratings come from only five people, all friends of the owner, who are not a fair sample of the customers
solve.work: Five reviews from friends: tiny, biased sample, not representative of customers.

questions.skill: Critiquing a graph or headline in the media
questions.stem: A bar graph shows two teams' wins: Team A has 18 and Team B has 20. The vertical axis starts at 16 instead of 0, so Team B's bar looks twice as tall as Team A's. What is misleading about the graph?
choices: The axis does not start at 0, which makes a small difference look large
The bars should have been drawn with exactly the same height for the two teams in the graph
The graph should have shown only Team B's wins, since Team B has the larger number of wins
Wins cannot be shown in a bar graph at all, and only a table can show them clearly
questions.answer: The axis does not start at 0, which makes a small difference look large
questions.solution: With the axis starting at 16, the bars are 2 and 4 units tall, so Team B looks twice as tall as Team A. The real numbers, 18 and 20, differ by only about 11 percent. A bar graph should start at 0.

solve.answer: The axis does not start at 0, which makes a small difference look large
solve.work: With axis from 16: bars show 2 and 4, so B looks twice A though 20/18 is about 1.11. Truncated axis exaggerates the difference.

questions.skill: Critiquing a graph or headline in the media
questions.stem: A headline says, "Chocolate helps you live longer!" The study was paid for by a candy company. Why does it matter who paid for the study?
choices: Studies that are paid for by a company are always wrong, so readers should ignore all of their findings
A study can only count as a real study if nobody at all pays for it, so this one cannot count
The payer may favor a certain result, so readers should look closely at how the study was done and what it showed
The payer decides what the numbers add up to in the study, so the results cannot be checked by anyone
questions.answer: The payer may favor a certain result, so readers should look closely at how the study was done and what it showed
questions.solution: Knowing who paid does not make a study wrong, but the payer may want a particular result. Readers should check how the data were collected and whether the conclusion is supported.

solve.answer: The payer may favor a certain result, so readers should look closely at how the study was done and what it showed
solve.work: Funding source is a possible conflict of interest; read methods and results carefully, not automatically reject.

questions.skill: Describing uncertainty in survey results
questions.stem: Why do reports of survey results often use words like "about" or "approximately"?
choices: The person who counted the answers was not sure how to count them, so the result is only a guess
Percents from a survey can only be written to the nearest ten, so they are never exact numbers
Reports must use those words whenever the survey was done on paper
A sample result is an estimate that may differ a little from the value for the whole group
questions.answer: A sample result is an estimate that may differ a little from the value for the whole group
questions.solution: A sample is only part of the whole group, so its result is an estimate. A different sample would probably give a slightly different value.

solve.answer: A sample result is an estimate that may differ a little from the value for the whole group
solve.work: Sample statistics estimate population values with sampling variability, hence 'about'.

questions.skill: Presenting conclusions clearly
questions.stem: A student makes a bar graph of the pet that each of the 30 students in Ms. Ray's class chose as a favorite. Which title tells readers the most about what the graph shows?
choices: Pets and Students in Ms. Ray's Class
Favorite Pet of the 30 Students in Ms. Ray's Class
Results of Our Survey in Ms. Ray's Class
A Graph of Data From Ms. Ray's Class
questions.answer: Favorite Pet of the 30 Students in Ms. Ray's Class
questions.solution: A good title says what was measured (favorite pet) and who was asked (the 30 students in Ms. Ray's class). The other titles leave out what was measured or say nothing about it.

solve.answer: Favorite Pet of the 30 Students in Ms. Ray's Class
solve.work: The most informative title names the variable (favorite pet), the group (30 students) and where (Ms. Ray's class). Only the first option does all of that.

questions.skill: Choosing a summary or display
questions.stem: A teacher has the test scores of 30 students. She wants a display that shows how many scores fall in each range, such as 60 to 69, 70 to 79 and 80 to 89. Which display fits best?
choices: A histogram
A scatter plot
A line graph of scores over time
A list of each student's name
questions.answer: A histogram
questions.solution: A histogram groups values into ranges and shows how many fall in each range. A scatter plot needs two measurements for each student, and a line graph over time needs scores recorded at different times.

solve.answer: A histogram
solve.work: Counts of scores in equal-width ranges (bins) is a histogram.

questions.skill: Critiquing a percent claim in the media
questions.stem: A headline says, "Car thefts fell by 120 percent this year!" Which statement explains the problem with this headline?
choices: A fall in thefts should always be reported as a number, never as a percent.
A percent can only describe an increase, never a decrease.
Thefts cannot fall by more than 100 percent, because that would mean fewer than zero thefts.
Any percent greater than 100 shows that the data were collected wrongly.
questions.answer: Thefts cannot fall by more than 100 percent, because that would mean fewer than zero thefts.
questions.solution: A fall of 100 percent means all of the thefts are gone, with zero left. A fall cannot be bigger than that, so 120 percent is impossible for a count. Percents can describe decreases, and percents over 100 are fine for increases.

solve.answer: Thefts cannot fall by more than 100 percent, because that would mean fewer than zero thefts.
solve.work: A 100% decrease takes thefts to zero; 120% would mean a negative count, impossible.

questions.skill: Critiquing an average in the media
questions.stem: A report says the mean number of children per family in a town is 2.4. Which statement is correct?
choices: At least one family must have exactly 2.4 children.
Most families must have exactly 2 children.
Every family must have 2 or 3 children.
No family can have exactly 2.4 children, yet the mean can still be 2.4.
questions.answer: No family can have exactly 2.4 children, yet the mean can still be 2.4.
questions.solution: A mean is found by adding and dividing, so it need not equal any family's actual number (no family can have 2.4 children). Families could have 0, 1, 4 or other numbers of children and still give a mean of 2.4.

solve.answer: No family can have exactly 2.4 children, yet the mean can still be 2.4.
solve.work: Counts of children are whole numbers, so no family has 2.4 children, but a mean of whole numbers can be 2.4 (e.g. total 24 children in 10 families). Other options do not follow from a mean.

questions.skill: Comparing groups with summary statistics
questions.stem: Team A's median score is 12 and Team B's median score is 15. Which conclusion does this support?
choices: Team B scored exactly 15 in every game.
Team B won more games than Team A.
At least half of Team B's scores were 15 or more.
Team B's highest score was 3 more than Team A's highest score.
questions.answer: At least half of Team B's scores were 15 or more.
questions.solution: The median is the middle value, so at least half of Team B's scores are 15 or higher. A median says nothing about every game, about winning, or about the highest score.

solve.answer: At least half of Team B's scores were 15 or more.
solve.work: A median of 15 means at least half the values are at or above 15. Nothing about every game, highest scores, or wins follows.

questions.skill: Critiquing a claim in the media
questions.stem: A student's report says, "More than half of the 25 students in our class prefer dogs." The votes were dogs 11, cats 8 and fish 6. What should a careful reader decide about the claim?
choices: Yes, because dogs got more votes than cats and more votes than fish
Yes, because 11 votes is close enough to half of the 25 students
No, because a class of only 25 students is too small to say anything
No, because dogs got 11 of the 25 votes, which is less than half
questions.answer: No, because dogs got 11 of the 25 votes, which is less than half
questions.solution: More than half of 25 students would be at least 13 students. Dogs got the most votes, but only 11, which is less than half. The claim is not supported. A small class is still enough to report what the class chose.

solve.answer: No, because dogs got 11 of the 25 votes, which is less than half
solve.work: Half of 25 is 12.5. Dogs got 11 < 12.5, so the claim of more than half is false. Option A gives the correct reason.

questions.skill: Critiquing a claim in the media
questions.stem: A report says, "Our test scores went up every year." The average scores were 70 in 2021, 74 in 2022, 73 in 2023 and 78 in 2024. Which statement about the claim is correct?
choices: It is supported, because the score in 2024 is higher than the score in 2021
It is not supported, because the average fell from 74 in 2022 to 73 in 2023
It is supported, because the scores rose in two of the three yearly changes
It cannot be judged, because averages never show how any one student did
questions.answer: It is not supported, because the average fell from 74 in 2022 to 73 in 2023
questions.solution: To go up every year, each score must be higher than the one before. The score fell from 74 to 73 between 2022 and 2023, so the claim is not supported even though the last score is the highest.

solve.answer: It is not supported, because the average fell from 74 in 2022 to 73 in 2023
solve.work: Changes: 70->74 up, 74->73 down, 73->78 up. 'Every year' fails because of the 2022-2023 drop. Option D.

questions.skill: Judge whether a claim in an ad can be trusted
questions.stem: An ad says, "9 out of 10 people we asked like our juice best." Which information would help you decide whether the claim can be trusted?
choices: What color the juice bottle is
How many seconds long the ad is
How many people were asked, and how they were picked
How much one bottle of juice costs
questions.answer: How many people were asked, and how they were picked
questions.solution: To trust "9 out of 10", you need to know about the survey itself: how many people were asked and how they were chosen. If only 10 friends of the company were asked, the claim says little. The color of the bottle, the length of the ad and the price do not tell you whether the survey was fair.

solve.answer: How many people were asked, and how they were picked
solve.work: Trusting a survey claim depends on the sample size and how the sample was chosen (e.g., only asking existing customers). Bottle color, price and ad length say nothing about the claim's reliability.

questions.skill: Limits of conclusions from an observational study
questions.stem: A study at one school finds that students who exercise more have higher grades. Which conclusion is best supported by the study?
choices: Exercise causes higher grades for all students in the country
Exercise and grades are associated here, but this does not show that exercise causes higher grades
Higher grades cause students to exercise more
Exercise has no effect on grades
questions.answer: Exercise and grades are associated here, but this does not show that exercise causes higher grades
questions.solution: The study found an association at one school. It does not show cause and effect in either direction, and it cannot speak for all students in the country.

solve.answer: Exercise and grades are associated here, but this does not show that exercise causes higher grades
solve.work: An observational study at one school shows association only, not causation, and cannot be generalized to the country.

questions.skill: Critiquing a percent-change claim
questions.stem: An ad says, "Our tutoring raised average quiz scores by 50 percent!" The average score went from 2 points to 3 points out of 100. Why is the claim misleading?
choices: A 50 percent increase is not possible with quiz scores
The score should have gone from 2 to 4 for a 50 percent increase
Percentages should never be used in advertising
A small starting value makes a gain of 1 point look like a large percent increase
questions.answer: A small starting value makes a gain of 1 point look like a large percent increase
questions.solution: Going from 2 to 3 is an increase of 1 point, which is $\frac{1}{2} = 50$ percent of the starting score, so the 50 percent is correct. But both scores are tiny out of 100, so the percent makes a very small gain sound large.

solve.answer: A small starting value makes a gain of 1 point look like a large percent increase
solve.work: 2 to 3 is indeed a 50 percent increase (1/2), but it is only 1 point out of 100; the small base makes the gain look large. Option 1 is false (2 to 4 is 100 percent).

questions.skill: Applying a sample result to a population
questions.stem: A report says that 18 of the 24 students in a sample improved. Suppose the same percent of all 600 students in the school improved. How many students would that be?
questions.solution: $\frac{18}{24} = 0.75$, which is 75 percent. 75 percent of 600 is $0.75 \times 600 = 450$ students.

questions.skill: Steps of a statistical investigation
questions.stem: Four actions from one investigation are numbered. 1: make a histogram of the results. 2: write the question "How many hours do students sleep?" 3: present the findings to the class. 4: measure the sleep hours of 30 students. The actions are put in the order in which they should happen. Which action number is third?
questions.solution: The order is: write the question (2), measure the sleep hours (4), make the histogram (1), present the findings (3). The third action in that order is number 1.

solve.work: Order: write the question (2), measure 30 students (4), make a histogram (1), present findings (3). Third in order is action 1.

questions.skill: Evaluating how data were collected
questions.stem: A researcher mails a survey to 500 households chosen at random. Only 200 households send it back. What percent of the households did not respond?
questions.solution: $500 - 200 = 300$ households did not respond. Then $300 \div 500 = 0.6$, which is 60 percent. With so many nonresponders, the answers may not represent all 500 households.

questions.skill: Choosing a summary or display
questions.stem: A company reports the salaries, in thousands of dollars, of 7 workers: 30, 32, 33, 35, 36, 38 and 250. Which measure best describes a typical salary?
choices: The median, because the value 250 pulls the mean far above most salaries
The mean, because it uses all seven values and so is always the best
The range, because it shows how much the largest salary exceeds the smallest
The highest salary, because it shows what the company is able to pay
questions.answer: The median, because the value 250 pulls the mean far above most salaries
questions.solution: The median is 35, close to most of the salaries. The mean is about 65 because the single value 250 pulls it up. For data with such an extreme value, the median describes a typical salary better.

solve.answer: The median, because the value 250 pulls the mean far above most salaries
solve.work: 250 is an outlier that pulls the mean to about 64.9; the median 35 is typical.

questions.skill: Critiquing a percent claim in the media
questions.stem: Last year a poll found that 42 percent of voters supported a measure. This year 51 percent support it. By how many percentage points did support rise?
questions.solution: Subtract the two percents: $51 - 42 = 9$ percentage points.

questions.skill: Critiquing a graph or headline in the media
questions.stem: A news story says, "Most car crashes involve drivers who ate breakfast that day." What question would best test whether this fact is meaningful?
choices: What color were most of the cars involved in the crashes?
What percent of all drivers ate breakfast that day?
How many people read the news story about the crashes?
What time of day did the story go to press?
questions.answer: What percent of all drivers ate breakfast that day?
questions.solution: If almost everyone eats breakfast, then most drivers in crashes will have eaten breakfast just by chance. The fact only means something when compared with the percent of all drivers who eat breakfast.

solve.answer: What percent of all drivers ate breakfast that day?
solve.work: Need the base rate: if most drivers eat breakfast anyway, the fact is meaningless.

questions.skill: Applying a sample result to a population
questions.stem: In a random sample of 80 trees, 6 were diseased. About how many diseased trees would you expect in a forest of 4,000 trees?
questions.solution: The diseased fraction in the sample is $6 \div 80 = 0.075$. Apply it to the forest: $0.075 \times 4000 = 300$ trees.

questions.skill: Applying a sample result to a population
questions.stem: A poll found that 45 percent of sampled households recycle. A town report applies this to the whole town and says about 1,350 households recycle. How many households are in the town?
questions.solution: If 45 percent of the town's households is 1,350, then the whole town is $1350 \div 0.45 = 3000$ households.

questions.skill: Describing uncertainty in survey results
questions.stem: A poll of a random sample reports that 52% of voters favor a plan, with a margin of error of 4 percentage points. According to the poll, what is the smallest percent of all voters who might favor the plan?
questions.solution: The margin of error means the true percent is probably within 4 percentage points of 52%. The lowest plausible value is $52 - 4 = 48$ percent.

questions.skill: Steps of a statistical investigation
questions.stem: While analyzing her data, Tia finds that 3 of the 40 surveys she collected were left blank. What is the best way to handle this in her investigation?
choices: Fill in the 3 blanks with the most common answer and say nothing about it in the report
Throw the 3 blank surveys away and write in the report that 40 students answered it
Report honestly that 3 of the surveys were blank and that the results are based on the other 37 surveys
Start over and survey a completely different group of 40 students without saying why
questions.answer: Report honestly that 3 of the surveys were blank and that the results are based on the other 37 surveys
questions.solution: A report should be honest about what data it used. Saying that 3 surveys were blank and that 37 were analyzed lets readers judge the results. Quietly filling in answers or claiming 40 answers hides what really happened.

solve.answer: Report honestly that 3 of the surveys were blank and that the results are based on the other 37 surveys
solve.work: Missing data should be reported openly; the analysis rests on the 37 completed surveys. The other options misreport or hide the problem.

questions.skill: Evaluating how data were collected
questions.stem: A radio show asks listeners to call in about whether the town should build a new park. Of the 400 callers, 85% say yes. Why can the show not report that 85% of the town wants the park?
choices: Percents are not allowed in reports about a whole town; the show may only report counts
Callers chose themselves, and people with strong opinions are the most likely to call
Four hundred people is too few for any survey of a town, even one chosen at random from the town
People who call a radio show are always older than the people in town, so the percent is too high
questions.answer: Callers chose themselves, and people with strong opinions are the most likely to call
questions.solution: People who call in volunteer, so the callers are not a random sample of the town. Those who care most are the most likely to call, which can push the percent up or down. A random sample of 400 could describe a town reasonably well.

solve.answer: Callers chose themselves, and people with strong opinions are the most likely to call
solve.work: Call-in poll is a voluntary-response sample: callers self-select and strong opinions are overrepresented, so 85% need not reflect the town.

questions.skill: Evaluating how data were collected
questions.stem: A student compares two brands of batteries. Brand X runs a toy in a cool room on Monday. Brand Y runs the toy in a warm room on Friday. Which change would make the comparison fairer?
choices: Test each brand a different number of times and then use whichever brand's total is larger
Use a different toy for each brand so that neither toy wears out from being used too much
Test both brands in the same room at the same temperature, using the same toy for each of the tests
Test only the brand that costs less, because the cheaper brand is the one most people buy
questions.answer: Test both brands in the same room at the same temperature, using the same toy for each of the tests
questions.solution: For a fair comparison, the only difference between the two tests should be the brand. Keeping the room, temperature and toy the same removes other explanations for any difference in running time.

solve.answer: Test both brands in the same room at the same temperature, using the same toy for each of the tests
solve.work: Confounding conditions (room temperature, day) differ. Fair comparison controls them: same room, same temperature, same toy.

questions.skill: Reporting results accurately
questions.stem: In a random sample of 40 eighth graders, the mean sleep time was 8.2 hours per night. Which is the best way to report this?
choices: The sample mean was 8.2 hours, so the mean for all eighth graders is probably close to 8.2 hours.
All eighth graders sleep exactly 8.2 hours every night, since the random sample of 40 eighth graders shows that.
Each of the 40 students in the sample slept exactly 8.2 hours every night, as the sample mean of 8.2 shows.
The true mean for all eighth graders is probably higher than 8.2 hours, since the sample was small.
questions.answer: The sample mean was 8.2 hours, so the mean for all eighth graders is probably close to 8.2 hours.
questions.solution: A sample mean is an estimate. It is probably close to the mean of all eighth graders, but it need not be exact, and it does not say each student slept 8.2 hours. A small sample does not tell us the true mean is higher.

solve.answer: The sample mean was 8.2 hours, so the mean for all eighth graders is probably close to 8.2 hours.
solve.work: A random sample mean estimates the population mean; it is probably close to 8.2 but not exact. No reason to think it is higher; individuals vary.

questions.skill: Reporting results accurately
questions.stem: Two classes took the same quiz. Class A had a mean of 80 and a range of 10 points. Class B had a mean of 80 and a range of 60 points. Which report describes the results best?
choices: The two classes did exactly the same, since both have a mean of 80 and the mean describes it.
Class B did better than Class A, since its range of 60 points is larger than Class A's range.
Class A did worse than Class B, since its range of 10 points is smaller than Class B's range.
Both classes averaged 80 points, but Class B's scores were much more spread out than Class A's scores were.
questions.answer: Both classes averaged 80 points, but Class B's scores were much more spread out than Class A's scores were.
questions.solution: Equal means show the classes had the same average, but the ranges show how spread out the scores were. A larger range means more spread, not higher scores, so Class B has more variation than Class A.

solve.answer: Both classes averaged 80 points, but Class B's scores were much more spread out than Class A's scores were.
solve.work: Same mean, different spread: B's scores are much more variable. Range doesn't say who did better.

questions.skill: Limits of conclusions
questions.stem: Which study could best show that a new fertilizer makes tomato plants grow taller?
choices: Randomly assign plants to get the fertilizer or no fertilizer, then compare the heights of the two groups
Ask gardeners who bought the fertilizer whether they think their plants grew tall this year
Measure plants in gardens of people who chose the fertilizer and compare them with other gardens
Compare the heights of the tallest plants found in several different gardens around the town
questions.answer: Randomly assign plants to get the fertilizer or no fertilizer, then compare the heights of the two groups
questions.solution: Random assignment makes the two groups alike apart from the fertilizer, so a difference in height can be credited to it. Asking buyers or comparing gardens leaves other explanations, such as better soil or more careful gardeners.

solve.answer: Randomly assign plants to get the fertilizer or no fertilizer, then compare the heights of the two groups
solve.issues: Leans toward study design rather than communicating results, though it bears on what conclusions a study can support.
solve.work: Causation needs a randomized experiment: randomly assign plants to fertilizer or none, compare heights. Others are observational or opinion.

questions.skill: Limits of conclusions
questions.stem: In an experiment, 60 adults aged 25 to 40 were randomly assigned to take a vitamin or a sugar pill. After a month, the vitamin group reported fewer colds. What is the best limit to put on the conclusion?
choices: Vitamins probably prevent colds in people of every age, since the groups were assigned at random.
The result means nothing at all, because a sugar pill was used instead of no pill in the study.
Vitamins cannot have helped, since the adults chose to join the study instead of being picked by chance.
The result may apply to adults like those studied, but not necessarily to children or older adults.
questions.answer: The result may apply to adults like those studied, but not necessarily to children or older adults.
questions.solution: Random assignment lets the result be credited to the vitamin for people like those studied. We cannot be sure it applies to children or older adults, who were not in the study. The sugar pill is what makes the comparison fair.

solve.answer: The result may apply to adults like those studied, but not necessarily to children or older adults.
solve.work: Random assignment supports cause within the studied group, but generalization is limited to similar adults (25-40). Placebo control is good, not a flaw.

questions.skill: Limits of conclusions
questions.stem: Cities with more firefighters tend to have more fire damage. A reporter writes, "Firefighters cause more fire damage." What is the best response?
choices: Large cities probably have both more firefighters and more fires, so the pattern does not show cause.
The reporter is right, because the pattern in the data is clear and more firefighters go with more damage.
The reporter is probably wrong, because the data show no pattern at all
The reporter should instead say that fire damage probably makes cities grow larger, since the two rise together.
questions.answer: Large cities probably have both more firefighters and more fires, so the pattern does not show cause.
questions.solution: The pattern is real, but a third factor, the size of the city, probably explains it: larger cities have more firefighters and more fires. A pattern alone does not show that one thing causes the other.

solve.answer: Large cities probably have both more firefighters and more fires, so the pattern does not show cause.
solve.work: City size is a lurking variable: big cities have more firefighters and more fires/damage. Association does not show cause.

questions.skill: Limits of conclusions
questions.stem: A plant's height was measured each week for 5 weeks: 3, 6, 9, 12 and 15 centimeters. A student writes, "In 40 weeks the plant will be 120 centimeters tall." What is the best comment on this claim?
choices: It is certain to be true, since the heights increase by exactly 3 centimeters every single week.
It assumes the weekly growth pattern continues far beyond the weeks that were measured.
It is unfair, since a plant cannot be measured more than once and then used to predict its height.
It would be correct only if the plant were measured in meters instead of in centimeters each week.
questions.answer: It assumes the weekly growth pattern continues far beyond the weeks that were measured.
questions.solution: The data cover only 5 weeks. Predicting far outside that range assumes the same steady growth continues, which may not happen because plants stop growing, so the claim is not certain.

solve.answer: It assumes the weekly growth pattern continues far beyond the weeks that were measured.
solve.work: Growth 3 cm/week; 3*40 = 120 so the arithmetic matches a linear model h=3w, but it extrapolates far beyond the 5 weeks observed; plants stop growing linearly.

questions.skill: Choosing a summary or display
questions.stem: A coach wants to show whether hours of practice and free-throw scores seem to be related for 15 players. Which display is best?
choices: A pie chart in which each slice shows one player's free-throw score out of the total
A bar graph that shows only the mean practice time of the 15 players on the team
A line plot of only the players' free-throw scores
A scatter plot with one point for each player, using practice hours and score
questions.answer: A scatter plot with one point for each player, using practice hours and score
questions.solution: To see whether two numbers are related, each player gives a pair (practice hours, score), and a scatter plot shows all the pairs together. The other displays show only one of the two variables or only a single summary.

solve.answer: A scatter plot with one point for each player, using practice hours and score
solve.work: Relationship between two quantitative variables per player: scatter plot (practice hours vs score).

questions.skill: Critiquing a percent claim in the media
questions.stem: An ad says, "Our running shoes cut injuries by 50 percent!" In the test, 2 of 40 runners in the new shoes were injured, and 4 of 40 runners in the old shoes were injured. What is the best critique?
choices: The groups were so small that a difference of 2 injuries could easily happen by chance
The ad is wrong, because injuries went down by only 2 percent
Injuries cannot be compared unless each group has exactly 100 runners
The ad should say 100 percent instead, since the new shoes had fewer injuries than the old shoes did
questions.answer: The groups were so small that a difference of 2 injuries could easily happen by chance
questions.solution: Going from 4 injuries to 2 is a 50 percent drop, so the arithmetic is right. But a difference of just 2 injuries in groups of 40 could happen by chance, so the test is too small to be convincing.

solve.answer: The groups were so small that a difference of 2 injuries could easily happen by chance
solve.work: Injury rates 4/40=10% vs 2/40=5%: relative cut 50% (ad's arithmetic is right), absolute 5 points. But the difference is only 2 injuries in small groups, easily due to chance. B is wrong (5 points, not 2).

questions.skill: Critiquing a percent claim in the media
questions.stem: A cereal box says, "Now with 25% less sugar!" What do you most need to know to judge the claim?
choices: How much the box costs compared with last year's box of the same kind of cereal at the store
How many people in the town eat cereal for breakfast
How many different colors appear on the front of the cereal box that carries the claim
Less than what: how much sugar the old cereal and the new cereal contain per serving
questions.answer: Less than what: how much sugar the old cereal and the new cereal contain per serving
questions.solution: A percent less is only meaningful against a starting amount. The sugar in the old and new cereal per serving show whether 25 percent less is a big change or a tiny one.

solve.answer: Less than what: how much sugar the old cereal and the new cereal contain per serving
solve.work: A relative claim needs its base: the old and new sugar amounts per serving.

questions.skill: Critiquing an average in the media
questions.stem: A restaurant says, "Our average wait time is 5 minutes." Last night's waits were 1, 1, 2, 2 and 19 minutes. Why might the claim mislead?
choices: The mean cannot be found for five waits that differ so much
Five waits are too few to find an average of at all
The average should have been the longest wait, which was 19 minutes, to show what a guest may face
One very long wait raised the mean, and most waits were 2 minutes or less
questions.answer: One very long wait raised the mean, and most waits were 2 minutes or less
questions.solution: The total is 25 minutes for 5 waits, so the mean is 5 minutes. But four of the five waits were 2 minutes or less. One long wait of 19 minutes pulls the mean up, so the median of 2 minutes describes the usual wait better.

solve.answer: One very long wait raised the mean, and most waits were 2 minutes or less
solve.work: Mean = (1+1+2+2+19)/5 = 25/5 = 5. One outlier (19) raises the mean; 4 of 5 waits were 2 min or less (median 2).

questions.skill: Critiquing a graph or headline in the media
questions.stem: A company says, "Our stock price rose 40% in three weeks!" The price had dropped 50% in the three months before that. What is the best critique?
choices: The price cannot rise by 40 percent after it has fallen
Three weeks is always too short a time for any claim about a price
The claim should be given in dollars rather than in percents, since percents can never describe a price
The claim shows only a short stretch of time that makes the change look good
questions.answer: The claim shows only a short stretch of time that makes the change look good
questions.solution: The claim picks one short period that looks good and leaves out the earlier drop. A 40 percent rise after a 50 percent fall still leaves the price well below where it started, so the fuller time period matters.

solve.answer: The claim shows only a short stretch of time that makes the change look good
solve.work: After -50% then +40%: 0.5*1.4 = 0.7, still 30% below. The claim cherry-picks a short window.

questions.skill: Critiquing a graph or headline in the media
questions.stem: A study of 300 adults found that people who drink more water tend to report better moods. Which headline is best supported by the study?
choices: People who drink more water tend to report better moods, study finds
Water is the only cure for a bad mood in any adult who tries it, study finds
Happier people never drink less water, study finds
Everyone who drinks more water will become happier than before, study finds
questions.answer: People who drink more water tend to report better moods, study finds
questions.solution: The study found a tendency, a pattern in the group studied. It does not show a cure, a rule with no exceptions, or a promise for everyone, so the headline must stay with the pattern.

solve.answer: People who drink more water tend to report better moods, study finds
solve.work: Observational association only; headline should state the tendency without cause or absolutes.

questions.skill: Describing uncertainty in survey results
questions.stem: Two random samples of 100 students each were taken from the same school. In one sample 48% prefer a later start, and in the other 55% do. What is the best explanation for the difference?
