choices: One of the two surveys must have been done incorrectly, because correct surveys give the same result
Different random samples include different students, so their results vary naturally
The students' opinions must have changed between the first sample and the second sample taken
The sample with the higher percent shows the true value for the school, and the other is too low
questions.answer: Different random samples include different students, so their results vary naturally
questions.solution: Each random sample contains different students, so results differ a little from sample to sample even when both are done correctly. Neither one has to be wrong, and neither is guaranteed to be the true value.

solve.answer: Different random samples include different students, so their results vary naturally
solve.work: Sampling variability: different random samples give different results; 48% vs 55% is plausible natural variation for n=100.

questions.skill: Steps of a statistical investigation
questions.stem: Before surveying the whole school about lunch, a student asks three friends to try out a draft of the survey and to say which questions are confusing. Their answers will not be counted in the results. Which step of a statistical investigation is she working on?
choices: Analyzing the data that were collected
Communicating the conclusions of the study
Planning how the data will be collected
Collecting the data that will be used in the results
questions.answer: Planning how the data will be collected
questions.solution: The three friends are only testing the draft, and their answers are not part of the results. Improving a survey before it is used is part of planning how the data will be collected.

solve.answer: Planning how the data will be collected
solve.work: Trying a draft survey on three friends whose answers are not counted is a pilot test, part of planning how data will be collected. Not collection of results, not analysis, not communication.

questions.skill: Reporting results accurately
questions.stem: A survey asked 80 students about homework. Twenty students skipped the question about time. Of the 60 students who answered, 30 said they spend more than an hour a night on homework. Which sentence reports this result most accurately?
choices: Half of the 80 students surveyed said they spend more than an hour a night on homework.
Half of all students at the school spend more than an hour a night on homework.
About 38 percent of the 60 students who answered said they spend more than an hour a night.
Half of the 60 students who answered said they spend more than an hour a night on homework.
questions.answer: Half of the 60 students who answered said they spend more than an hour a night on homework.
questions.solution: Only 60 students answered the question, and 30 of them is half. Saying half of the 80 surveyed is wrong, because 30 of 80 is 37.5 percent. Saying 38 percent of the 60 who answered uses the wrong base. The sample cannot be stretched to every student in the school.

solve.answer: Half of the 60 students who answered said they spend more than an hour a night on homework.
solve.work: 30 of 60 who answered = 50% = half of those who answered. Not half of the school (no basis), not half of 80 (30/80 = 37.5%), and 38% is 30/80 wrongly applied to the 60.

questions.skill: Choosing a summary or display
questions.stem: A report on the prices of 40 homes uses the median to describe the center, because a few very expensive homes pull the mean up. Which measure of spread should the report pair with the median?
choices: The standard deviation
The interquartile range
The mean
The mode
questions.answer: The interquartile range
questions.solution: The median is paired with the interquartile range, which is not pulled by a few extreme values. The standard deviation is paired with the mean. The mean and the mode are measures of center, not of spread.

solve.answer: The interquartile range
solve.work: With a skewed distribution and the median as center, the resistant measure of spread is the interquartile range. Standard deviation pairs with the mean; mode and mean are not spreads.

questions.skill: Critiquing a percent claim in the media
questions.stem: A store sign says, "Save up to 70 percent on everything!" Which conclusion does the sign support?
choices: Every item is discounted by exactly 70 percent.
No item is discounted by more than 70 percent, and some may be discounted by much less.
The average discount on all of the items is at least 70 percent.
Every item is discounted by at least 35 percent.
questions.answer: No item is discounted by more than 70 percent, and some may be discounted by much less.
questions.solution: "Up to 70 percent" gives only the largest possible discount. Other items may be discounted by much less, so the sign does not tell you the discount on any particular item or the average discount.

solve.answer: No item is discounted by more than 70 percent, and some may be discounted by much less.
solve.work: 'Up to 70 percent' gives a maximum discount only; it says nothing about a minimum or the average. So no item exceeds 70% and some may be much less.

questions.skill: Critiquing an average in the media
questions.stem: A tutor writes, "Students here average 40 minutes of homework a night." The tutor's data are 20, 25, 30, 35 and 90 minutes. Which statement about the claim is best?
choices: The mean is 40, but four of the five students do less than 40 minutes, so 40 is not typical.
The mean is not 40, because adding the times and dividing by 5 gives 30.
The claim is fair because most of the students do 40 minutes or more.
The claim is fair because a mean always describes a typical student.
questions.answer: The mean is 40, but four of the five students do less than 40 minutes, so 40 is not typical.
questions.solution: The sum is 20 + 25 + 30 + 35 + 90 = 200, and 200 divided by 5 is 40, so the mean is 40. But the 90 pulls the mean up: four of the five students do less than 40 minutes, and the median is 30. The report should say so.

solve.answer: The mean is 40, but four of the five students do less than 40 minutes, so 40 is not typical.
solve.work: Sum 20+25+30+35+90 = 200; 200/5 = 40, so the mean is 40. Four of five values are below 40; the 90 outlier pulls the mean up, so 40 is not typical (median 30).

questions.skill: Comparing groups with summary statistics
questions.stem: Group X's scores have a minimum of 10, a first quartile of 20, a median of 30, a third quartile of 40 and a maximum of 50. Group Y's scores have a minimum of 25, a first quartile of 28, a median of 30, a third quartile of 32 and a maximum of 35. Which statement compares the groups fairly?
choices: The medians are equal, but Group X's scores are more spread out: an interquartile range of 20 versus 4.
Group X did better, because its highest score and its range are both greater.
Group Y did better, because its scores are closer together than Group X's scores.
The two groups are the same, because their medians are equal and nothing else matters.
questions.answer: The medians are equal, but Group X's scores are more spread out: an interquartile range of 20 versus 4.
questions.solution: Both medians are 30. The interquartile range is 40 - 20 = 20 for Group X and 32 - 28 = 4 for Group Y, so Group X is far more spread out. Having a greater range or closer scores does not mean doing better, and equal medians do not make the groups the same.

solve.answer: The medians are equal, but Group X's scores are more spread out: an interquartile range of 20 versus 4.
solve.work: Medians both 30. IQR X = 40-20 = 20; IQR Y = 32-28 = 4. Fair comparison: same center, X more spread out. Being less spread out is not 'better'.

questions.skill: Generalizing beyond the sample
questions.stem: A student surveys 30 classmates in her homeroom about screen time. She then states, "Students in our whole district spend about 3 hours a day on screens." Which is the best critique?
choices: Her homeroom was not a random sample of the district, so the claim may not apply to all students
She should have surveyed fewer students
Screen time cannot be measured in hours
She should have surveyed only students who use screens a lot
questions.answer: Her homeroom was not a random sample of the district, so the claim may not apply to all students
questions.solution: One homeroom is not chosen at random from the district, so it may differ from the other students. A conclusion about the whole district needs a sample that represents the district.

solve.answer: Her homeroom was not a random sample of the district, so the claim may not apply to all students
solve.work: One homeroom is a convenience sample, not random or representative of the district, so generalizing to the district is not justified.

questions.skill: Critiquing an average in the media
questions.stem: A news report says, "The average (mean) home price in the town is 450 thousand dollars." Most homes sold for about 200 thousand dollars, but a few very large homes sold for over 2 million dollars. Which is the best critique?
choices: The mean is always the best measure of a typical value
The report should have used the largest price instead
A few very expensive homes raise the mean, so the median would describe a typical home better
The report is correct because most homes cost 450 thousand dollars
questions.answer: A few very expensive homes raise the mean, so the median would describe a typical home better
questions.solution: The very expensive homes pull the mean far above what most homes cost. The median is not affected much by a few extreme values, so it describes a typical home better here.

solve.answer: A few very expensive homes raise the mean, so the median would describe a typical home better
solve.work: Right-skewed prices: a few very expensive homes pull the mean far above the typical 200 thousand; the median is a better measure of a typical home.

questions.skill: What a report should include
questions.stem: A student finishes a statistical investigation and writes a report for her class. Which should the report include so that readers can judge the conclusions fairly?
choices: Only the results that support her conclusion
Only the final conclusion, without how the data were collected
Her opinion of which classmates answered best
How the sample was chosen, how many were included, and what the data cannot show
questions.answer: How the sample was chosen, how many were included, and what the data cannot show
questions.solution: Readers need to know how the data were gathered and what the study can and cannot tell them. Leaving out opposing results or the method hides information they need.

solve.answer: How the sample was chosen, how many were included, and what the data cannot show
solve.work: A fair report states the sampling method, sample size and limitations; the other options hide information or add bias.

questions.skill: Reporting results accurately
questions.stem: A report says that 27% of the students in a sample preferred pizza. This was 108 students. How many students were in the sample?
questions.solution: If 27 percent of the sample is 108 students, then 1 percent is $108 \div 27 = 4$ students, and the whole sample is $4 \times 100 = 400$ students.

questions.skill: Limits of conclusions
questions.stem: A report concludes, "Coffee prevents this illness in people everywhere." It is based on an observational study of 500 adults chosen at random from one county. Consider four statements. (1) It claims a cause from an observational study. (2) The adults were chosen at random. (3) It applies the result to people beyond one county. (4) Five hundred is always too small a sample. How many of the four statements describe a flaw in the conclusion?
questions.solution: Statements 1 and 3 are flaws: an observational study cannot show cause, and a sample from one county cannot speak for people everywhere. Statement 2 is a strength, not a flaw. Statement 4 is not true, because 500 randomly chosen people can be a good sample. Two statements describe flaws.

solve.work: (1) causal claim from observational study: flaw. (2) random selection: a strength, not a flaw. (3) generalizing beyond one county: flaw. (4) 500 is not always too small: a false statement, not a flaw. Count = 2.

questions.skill: Choosing a summary or display
questions.stem: Of 50 sixth graders and 200 seventh graders surveyed, 20 sixth graders and 60 seventh graders like soccer best. To compare the two grades fairly in a report, what should be shown?
choices: Only the counts, 20 and 60, because they are the actual data
The total number of students surveyed in both grades, which is 250
The percent of each grade that likes soccer, which is 40% and 30%
The difference between the two counts, which is 40 students
questions.answer: The percent of each grade that likes soccer, which is 40% and 30%
questions.solution: The grades were different sizes, so counts alone mislead. Percents compare each grade to its own size: $20 \div 50 = 40\%$ of sixth graders and $60 \div 200 = 30\%$ of seventh graders.

solve.answer: The percent of each grade that likes soccer, which is 40% and 30%
solve.work: Group sizes differ, so compare relative frequencies: 20/50 = 40%, 60/200 = 30%. The percents in the option are correct.

questions.skill: Choosing a summary or display
questions.stem: In Group A, 18 of 24 plants grew taller than 10 centimeters. In Group B, 21 of 35 plants did. To compare the groups fairly, a report gives percents. By how many percentage points is Group A's percent higher than Group B's?
questions.solution: Group A: $18 \div 24 = 0.75$, or 75%. Group B: $21 \div 35 = 0.6$, or 60%. The difference is $75 - 60 = 15$ percentage points.

questions.skill: Critiquing a percent claim in the media
questions.stem: A poll found that support for a plan rose from 40% to 48%. A headline says, "Support jumps 20 percent!" Which statement describes the change accurately in both ways?
choices: Support rose 20 percentage points, which is an 8 percent increase over the old 40%
Support rose 8 percent, which is a 20 percentage point increase from the old 40%
Support rose 8 percentage points, which is a 20 percent increase over the old 40%
Support rose 8 percentage points, which is an 8 percent increase over the old 40%
questions.answer: Support rose 8 percentage points, which is a 20 percent increase over the old 40%
questions.solution: The difference between 48% and 40% is 8 percentage points. Compared with the old 40%, that is $8 \div 40 = 0.2$, a 20 percent increase. Percentage points and percent are different ways to describe the change.

solve.answer: Support rose 8 percentage points, which is a 20 percent increase over the old 40%

questions.skill: Critiquing a percent claim in the media
questions.stem: A news story says, "The sales tax rose only 1 percent." The rate actually went from 5 percent to 6 percent. By what percent did the tax rate itself increase?
questions.solution: The rate rose by 1 percentage point. Compared with the old rate of 5 percent, that is $1 \div 5 = 0.2$, which is a 20 percent increase in the rate itself.

questions.skill: Critiquing a percent claim in the media
questions.stem: A store raised the price of a game by 20 percent, then advertised a 20 percent price cut, saying prices are "back where they started." The original price was 50 dollars. What is the price after the cut, in dollars?
questions.solution: After the 20 percent rise the price is $50 \times 1.2 = 60$ dollars. A 20 percent cut of 60 dollars takes off 12 dollars, leaving 48 dollars. It is not back to 50 dollars, because the 20 percent was taken from a larger amount.

solve.work: 50 x 1.2 = 60; 60 x 0.8 = 48 dollars, not back to 50.

questions.skill: Critiquing an average in the media
questions.stem: A report says the mean score of the 20 students in Class A is 80, and the mean score of the 30 students in Class B is 70. A headline says, "The two classes together average 75." What is the actual mean score of all 50 students?
questions.solution: Add up all the points. Class A has $20 \times 80 = 1600$ and Class B has $30 \times 70 = 2100$, so the total is 3700 points. Divide by 50 students: $3700 \div 50 = 74$. The mean is not 75 because Class B has more students.

solve.work: Weighted mean: (20 x 80 + 30 x 70)/50 = (1600 + 2100)/50 = 3700/50 = 74. The headline's 75 wrongly averages the two means.

questions.skill: Critiquing a graph or headline in the media
questions.stem: A bar graph's vertical axis starts at 40 instead of 0. One bar shows 44 and another bar shows 48. The taller bar looks how many times as tall as the shorter bar?
questions.solution: Bar heights are measured from the start of the axis. The bars are $44 - 40 = 4$ units and $48 - 40 = 8$ units tall, so the taller bar looks $8 \div 4 = 2$ times as tall, though the real values differ by less than 10 percent.

questions.skill: Critiquing a graph or headline in the media
questions.stem: A headline says Town B is more dangerous than Town A because it had more accidents. Town A had 30 accidents and has 10,000 residents. Town B had 45 accidents and has 20,000 residents. How many more accidents per 1,000 residents did Town A have than Town B?
questions.solution: Town A: $30 \div 10 = 3$ accidents per 1,000 residents. Town B: $45 \div 20 = 2.25$ per 1,000. The difference is $3 - 2.25 = 0.75$. Town A is actually worse once the towns' sizes are taken into account.

questions.skill: Applying a sample result to a population
questions.stem: To estimate the number of fish in a pond, 40 fish were caught, tagged and released. Later a sample of 50 fish was caught, and 5 of them had tags. If the sample is typical of the pond, about how many fish are in the pond?
questions.solution: In the sample, $5 \div 50 = 0.1$, so about 10 percent of the fish are tagged. The 40 tagged fish are about 10 percent of the pond, so the pond holds about $40 \div 0.1 = 400$ fish.

questions.skill: Applying a sample result to a population
questions.stem: In a district sample, 33 of 60 eighth graders and 24 of 40 seventh graders want an earlier start. The district has 300 eighth graders and 250 seventh graders. If the samples are typical, about how many students in these two grades want an earlier start?
questions.solution: Eighth grade: $33 \div 60 = 0.55$ and $0.55 \times 300 = 165$. Seventh grade: $24 \div 40 = 0.6$ and $0.6 \times 250 = 150$. The total is $165 + 150 = 315$ students.

questions.skill: Describing uncertainty in survey results
questions.stem: A poll reports that the plausible percent of all voters who favor a plan runs from 41% to 49%. What percent of the sample favored the plan?
questions.solution: The plausible values are centered on the sample percent, with the margin of error on each side. The center is the middle of 41 and 49: $(41 + 49) \div 2 = 45$ percent. The margin of error is 4 percentage points.

solve.work: The interval is the sample percent +/- margin; midpoint (41 + 49)/2 = 45.

questions.skill: Steps of a statistical investigation
questions.stem: After analyzing her data, Jo sees that her survey asked only about weekdays, but her question was about how much students read each week. What is the best next step?
choices: Report the weekday results as if they covered the whole week
Collect weekend data as well, or report that the results describe weekdays only
Multiply the weekday mean by 7 and call that the weekly mean, with no weekend data at all
Change the question to match the data without telling readers
questions.answer: Collect weekend data as well, or report that the results describe weekdays only
questions.solution: The data do not cover the whole question. Jo can either collect the missing weekend data or be clear that the results cover weekdays only. Pretending the data cover the week, or guessing the rest by multiplying, or quietly changing the question, would mislead readers.

solve.answer: Collect weekend data as well, or report that the results describe weekdays only
solve.work: The data do not cover the question's scope (whole week). Either collect weekend data or limit the conclusion to weekdays. Others hide or distort the limitation (x7 assumes weekend = weekday).

questions.skill: Steps of a statistical investigation
questions.stem: A class finishes an investigation and evaluates its process. Which statement is the strongest evaluation?
choices: The study was good because the results matched what we expected before collecting data, so we will repeat it as is
Only seventh graders were asked, so the results may not fit the school; we will sample every grade next time
The study was good because we made five different graphs, so we will keep the same method
Nothing needs to improve because every student we asked answered the question fully, so we will do it the same way again
questions.answer: Only seventh graders were asked, so the results may not fit the school; we will sample every grade next time
questions.solution: A good evaluation names a specific weakness in the process and how to fix it. Matching expectations, drawing many graphs, or getting complete answers does not show that the sample or method was sound.

solve.answer: Only seventh graders were asked, so the results may not fit the school; we will sample every grade next time
solve.work: A strong evaluation names a real weakness (sample only seventh graders, not representative of the school) and an improvement. Others use irrelevant criteria (number of graphs, matching expectations, full answers).

questions.skill: Steps of a statistical investigation
questions.stem: A student's report lists the question, the data table and the conclusion, but leaves out how the 25 students were chosen. Why is this a weakness?
choices: Without it, readers cannot tell what question the report was trying to answer or why it was asked
Without the method, nobody can calculate the mean or the median of the values in the data table
Readers cannot judge whether the 25 students fairly represent the group the conclusion is about
Without it, the conclusion must be changed to the opposite of what the data in the table actually show
questions.answer: Readers cannot judge whether the 25 students fairly represent the group the conclusion is about
questions.solution: How the sample was chosen tells readers whether it can speak for a larger group. The missing method does not stop anyone from computing a mean or median, and it does not reverse the conclusion.

solve.answer: Readers cannot judge whether the 25 students fairly represent the group the conclusion is about
solve.work: The sampling method determines whether the sample represents the population. Omitting it means readers cannot judge representativeness. Means can still be computed; the question is listed; conclusion need not flip.

questions.skill: Evaluating how data were collected
questions.stem: A district emails a survey about a later school start to every family. Only 12% of families reply, and most replies say they want a later start. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: The replies match all families, because the survey was sent to every family and so nobody was left out
The replies match all families, because most of the replies said the same thing
The replies are useless, because surveys must always be given in person
The replies may not match all families, since few replied and those who did may feel strongly
questions.answer: The replies may not match all families, since few replied and those who did may feel strongly
questions.solution: Sending a survey to everyone does not help if only 12% answer. Families with strong opinions are more likely to reply, so the replies may differ from the opinions of all families. Surveys do not have to be in person to give useful information.

solve.answer: The replies may not match all families, since few replied and those who did may feel strongly
solve.work: 12% response rate means nonresponse bias is possible; those who replied may feel strongly. Sending to all does not make replies representative.

questions.skill: Evaluating how data were collected
questions.stem: A teacher gives a new study app to her morning class and not to her afternoon class. The morning class scores higher on the next test. What flaw in the process makes it hard to credit the app?
choices: Only two groups were compared, and an investigation always needs at least five groups to be fair
The test should have been given to the morning class alone, because the afternoon class did not use the app
Students were not assigned to the groups at random, so the classes may have differed in other ways
A new app can never change the scores that students earn, so no study could ever give credit to an app
questions.answer: Students were not assigned to the groups at random, so the classes may have differed in other ways
questions.solution: The classes may differ in many ways, such as ability or time of day. Without random assignment, a higher score could come from those differences instead of the app. Comparing two groups is the usual design, and an app can change scores.

solve.answer: Students were not assigned to the groups at random, so the classes may have differed in other ways
solve.work: Groups were existing classes (morning vs afternoon), not randomly assigned, so other differences (time of day, students) are confounded with the app.

questions.skill: Reporting results accurately
questions.stem: A report says, "The survey proves that most students like math." The survey asked 25 students in an advanced math class, and 18 said they like math. Which rewrite is best?
choices: Most students in every math class at the school like math, since 18 of the 25 students asked in one class said so.
Of the 25 students in an advanced math class, 18 said they like math; other classes might answer differently.
Of the 25 students, 72 percent like math, so 72 percent of the whole school likes math.
At least 18 students like math in each class at the school, as the survey of one class showed.
questions.answer: Of the 25 students in an advanced math class, 18 said they like math; other classes might answer differently.
questions.solution: The result only describes the 25 students who were asked, who are not a typical group. A fair rewrite says who was surveyed and admits that other groups might differ. The other statements claim more than the data show.

solve.answer: Of the 25 students in an advanced math class, 18 said they like math; other classes might answer differently.
solve.work: Sample is one advanced math class, not representative; 18/25 = 72%. Best rewrite reports what was found for that group and notes the limit.

questions.skill: Reporting results accurately
questions.stem: In random samples, 30% of 20 sixth graders and 30% of 200 seventh graders say they walk to school. Which statement is best?
choices: The two results are equally dependable, because the two percents are equal and both are from random samples.
The sixth-grade result is more dependable, because small groups give percents that are more exact than big ones.
The percents match, but the seventh-grade result rests on more students, so it is more dependable.
The two percents cannot be compared, because they come from different grades
questions.answer: The percents match, but the seventh-grade result rests on more students, so it is more dependable.
questions.solution: Equal percents do not mean equal dependability. A larger random sample usually gives an estimate closer to the value for the whole grade, so the seventh-grade result is more dependable. Percents from different grades can still be compared.

solve.answer: The percents match, but the seventh-grade result rests on more students, so it is more dependable.
solve.work: Same 30%, but n=200 gives less sampling variability than n=20, so the seventh-grade estimate is more dependable.

questions.skill: Limits of conclusions
questions.stem: An observational study finds that students who attend optional tutoring score 10 points higher on average than students who do not. Why can we not conclude that tutoring caused the higher scores?
choices: Ten points is too small a difference to count as higher in any study, however it was carried out.
Tutoring never changes a student's scores, so the study of the two groups must have been done wrong.
Studies of scores must include every student in the whole country before any conclusion can be drawn.
Students who choose tutoring may be more motivated, and that motivation could also be what raises their scores.
questions.answer: Students who choose tutoring may be more motivated, and that motivation could also be what raises their scores.
questions.solution: The students chose whether to attend, so the two groups may differ in other ways, such as motivation. Those differences, not tutoring, could explain the gap. Only a study that assigns students at random can credit the tutoring itself.

solve.answer: Students who choose tutoring may be more motivated, and that motivation could also be what raises their scores.
solve.work: Observational study with self-selection: motivation is a confounder that could raise scores and lead to choosing tutoring.

questions.skill: Limits of conclusions
questions.stem: Survey A asked 1,000 students at a rock concert about their favorite music. Survey B asked 100 students chosen at random from the school's list of students. Which statement best compares them for describing the whole school?
choices: A is more dependable, since 1,000 students is many more than 100 students and a larger sample is better.
They are equally dependable, since both surveys asked students about music.
B is more dependable, since random choice avoids a bias that A's larger size cannot fix.
Neither says anything about the students at the school, since each is a sample.
questions.answer: B is more dependable, since random choice avoids a bias that A's larger size cannot fix.
questions.solution: Students at a rock concert are likely to prefer rock music, so Survey A is biased no matter how many were asked. A random sample of 100 from the school's list can describe the school. Size does not repair bias.

solve.answer: B is more dependable, since random choice avoids a bias that A's larger size cannot fix.
solve.work: Survey A is biased (rock concert attendees); size does not fix bias. B is a random sample of the school, so more dependable.

questions.skill: Choosing a summary or display
questions.stem: A data set has a mean of 40 and a median of 25. What does this most likely tell a reporter about the data?
choices: The data are symmetric, so the mean and the median describe the data equally well as a typical value
A few very large values pull the mean above the median, so the data are skewed to the high side
A few very small values pull the mean down, so the data are skewed to the low side of the values
The median must have been calculated incorrectly, since a median should never be smaller than the mean
questions.answer: A few very large values pull the mean above the median, so the data are skewed to the high side
questions.solution: A mean well above the median is a sign that a few large values are pulling the mean up. That is skewing to the high side. In that case the median is often a better description of a typical value.

solve.answer: A few very large values pull the mean above the median, so the data are skewed to the high side
solve.work: Mean (40) > median (25): a few large values pull the mean up; right (high) skew.

questions.skill: Critiquing an average in the media
questions.stem: A news story says the mean household income in a town rose from 60 thousand to 66 thousand dollars, and adds, "Everyone is better off." What is the best critique?
choices: The mean cannot rise unless the income of every household in the town rises by some amount as well
A rise in the mean can come from a few high incomes, so it does not show every household gained
Incomes cannot be averaged, because they are measured in dollars
The story should have reported only the largest income in the town, since it shows who is better off
questions.answer: A rise in the mean can come from a few high incomes, so it does not show every household gained
questions.solution: The mean can go up even when most incomes stay the same or fall, if a few incomes grow a lot. The median or a look at several groups would show whether typical households gained.

solve.answer: A rise in the mean can come from a few high incomes, so it does not show every household gained
solve.work: Mean rose by 6 thousand; this can come from a few households' big gains while others fall or stay. Does not show everyone gained.

questions.skill: Critiquing a graph or headline in the media
questions.stem: A graph shows a town's population with a picture of a person. The 2020 picture is 1 inch tall and 1 inch wide for 10 thousand people. The 2024 picture is 2 inches tall and 2 inches wide for 20 thousand people. Why is it misleading?
choices: A picture for a larger population should be drawn smaller than one for a smaller population, to fit the page
Pictures cannot be used to show the size of a population, only numbers written in a table can do that job well
Doubling height and width makes the picture look four times as large, though the population only doubled
Population should be shown only in whole numbers of thousands, never in tens of thousands as it is here in this graph
questions.answer: Doubling height and width makes the picture look four times as large, though the population only doubled
questions.solution: Doubling the height and the width makes the area $2 \times 2 = 4$ times as large, so the later picture seems to show four times the population, but the population only doubled from 10 thousand to 20 thousand.

solve.answer: Doubling height and width makes the picture look four times as large, though the population only doubled
solve.work: Scaling both dimensions by 2 makes area 4 times larger while population only doubled (10k to 20k): pictograph distortion.

questions.skill: Comparing groups with summary statistics
questions.stem: Group X has a mean of 82 and Group Y has a mean of 79. Group X has 3 students and Group Y has 30 students. A report says, "Group X outperforms Group Y." What is the best comment?
choices: Group X is clearly better than Group Y, since a mean of 82 is greater than a mean of 79
The gap is small, and Group X is so small that a single student's score could change its mean a lot
Group Y is better than Group X, since it has more students and so its total score is larger
Means cannot be compared when the groups have different sizes, so no comment can be made at all
questions.answer: The gap is small, and Group X is so small that a single student's score could change its mean a lot
questions.solution: A mean from only 3 students can change a lot with one score, so a 3-point gap says little. Means can still be compared for groups of different sizes, but a larger group gives a more dependable mean.

solve.answer: The gap is small, and Group X is so small that a single student's score could change its mean a lot
solve.work: Gap of 3 points; Group X has only 3 students, so one score shifts its mean a lot (one student changing by 9 points moves mean 3). Claim is weak.

questions.skill: Comparing groups with summary statistics
questions.stem: Two samples of 10 plants each have mean heights of 31.0 centimeters and 31.4 centimeters. In each sample, heights range from 20 to 42 centimeters. A report says, "Fertilizer B grows taller plants." What is the best critique?
choices: The 0.4 centimeter gap is tiny compared with the wide spread in each group, so it may be chance
Fertilizer B must work better, since 31.4 is greater than 31.0, and a greater mean always means a better fertilizer
Ten plants in each sample is too many; using fewer plants would give a much clearer comparison
Heights should be reported in meters, not centimeters
questions.answer: The 0.4 centimeter gap is tiny compared with the wide spread in each group, so it may be chance
questions.solution: Plants in each group differ by over 20 centimeters, so a difference of 0.4 centimeter between the means is small relative to that variation and could happen by chance. A greater mean alone does not prove a fertilizer works.

solve.answer: The 0.4 centimeter gap is tiny compared with the wide spread in each group, so it may be chance
solve.issues: Minor: stem never says which sample got fertilizer B; inferred from the 31.4 mean. Does not affect the answer.
solve.work: Difference 0.4 cm versus range 22 cm in each sample of 10: the difference is easily explained by chance variation.

questions.skill: Describing uncertainty in survey results
questions.stem: A poll reports that 52% of voters favor Plan A, with a margin of error of 4 percentage points. Can the poll say that a majority of all voters favor Plan A?
choices: Not with certainty, since the plausible values run from 48% to 56%, a range that includes values below 50%
Yes, since 52% is greater than 50%, the poll shows for certain that Plan A has the votes of a majority
Yes, since a margin of error of 4 percentage points only matters when a poll's result is below 50%
No, since a poll of some voters can never tell us anything about all voters, even with a margin of error
questions.answer: Not with certainty, since the plausible values run from 48% to 56%, a range that includes values below 50%
questions.solution: The margin of error gives plausible values from $52 - 4 = 48\%$ to $52 + 4 = 56\%$. Since that range includes numbers below 50%, the poll cannot say with certainty that a majority favor Plan A. Polls do tell us something, but with uncertainty.

solve.answer: Not with certainty, since the plausible values run from 48% to 56%, a range that includes values below 50%
solve.work: 52% +/- 4 gives 48% to 56%; includes values below 50%, so a majority is not established with confidence.

questions.skill: Evaluating how data were collected
questions.stem: A student asks 100 classmates, in a crowded hallway where others can hear, "Have you ever copied homework from a friend?" Only 3 of them say yes. Which limit should her report mention?
choices: Students may not answer honestly when others can hear, so the true percent may be higher than 3 percent
A result as small as 3 percent is too small to report, so the study must be repeated again
Asking in a hallway makes the sample random, so the report does not need to state any limits
The question was about homework, so the result also applies to every other kind of schoolwork
questions.answer: Students may not answer honestly when others can hear, so the true percent may be higher than 3 percent
questions.solution: People often hold back an answer about something embarrassing when others can hear. A report should say that this way of asking may have made the result too low. Small percents can be reported, a hallway does not make a sample random, and the result only covers the question that was asked.

solve.answer: Students may not answer honestly when others can hear, so the true percent may be higher than 3 percent
solve.work: A sensitive question asked where others can hear invites dishonest 'no' answers (response bias), so the true rate is likely higher than 3%. Other options are false: generalizing beyond homework, hallway is not random, small results can be reported.

questions.skill: Critiquing an average in the media
questions.stem: A cafe sold these numbers of cups of tea on six days: 20, 22, 24, 26, 28 and 180. The 180 was the day a school trip visited. The mean is 50 and the median is 25. A writer wants readers to understand both what a normal day is like and why the mean is so high. Which report does both accurately?
choices: The mean of 50 cups is a fair picture of a normal day, because it uses all six days of sales
A normal day sells about 25 cups, and the 180 was a mistake, so it should be left out
The school-trip day shows what the cafe can really sell, so the other five days were unusually slow
Five ordinary days sold 20 to 28 cups; one school-trip day sold 180 and pulled the mean up to 50
questions.answer: Five ordinary days sold 20 to 28 cups; one school-trip day sold 180 and pulled the mean up to 50
questions.solution: The five ordinary days total 120, a mean of 24. With the 180 the total is 300 and the mean is $300 / 6 = 50$, higher than five of the six days. An honest report gives the usual level and says that one real, unusual day raised the mean. The 180 was a real day, not a mistake, and it should not be hidden.

solve.answer: Five ordinary days sold 20 to 28 cups; one school-trip day sold 180 and pulled the mean up to 50
solve.work: Check: 20+22+24+26+28 = 120, +180 = 300, /6 = 50; median (24+26)/2 = 25. Option A describes normal days (20-28) and explains the outlier pulling the mean to 50. B misrepresents a normal day; C calls a real value a mistake; D misreads normal days as slow.
